title: Discovering Undisclosed Concepts in LoRA Adapters for Diffusion-Based AIGC Models
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has made diffusion model personalization affordable and widely shareable, but it also creates moderation risks when harmful or problematic content is not faithfully disclosed. Hence, it is desired to develop a mechanism that, given a LoRA adapter, discovers the concept it was trained to generate, so as to support downstream investigation. We characterize the target concept through the conditioning input that most clearly exposes what the LoRA has learned. Such an input should induce coherent LoRA outputs that are distinctive from those of the base model and strongly align with the learned LoRA subspace. We therefore formulate concept discovery as searching for the conditioning input that jointly maximizes output coherence, LoRA-induced distinctiveness, and subspace alignment. Even with a clear objective, however, optimizing it over an open-ended input space is prohibitively expensive, since reliable evaluation of coherence and distinctiveness requires repeated diffusion rendering. Crucially, we observe that an input need not be rendered to determine whether it is promising. Its alignment with the learned LoRA subspace provides a lightweight signal for localizing promising candidates before visual verification. Based on this insight, we develop a two-stage framework for text-to-image LoRAs. Subspace-Guided Evolutionary Search (SGES) uses render-free subspace alignment to explore candidate prompts and retain a compact shortlist, while Paired Visual Identification (PVI) renders only these candidates and compares the LoRA and base-model outputs to identify those exhibiting coherent and distinctive generation behavior. This design enables efficient and reliable discovery of previously unknown concepts encoded in LoRA adapters.

title: MultiAlloc: Budget-Aware Precision Allocation for KV Cache Quantization
abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.

title: Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal
abstract: Although language is predominantly spoken, empirical tests of surprisal theory rely almost entirely on written text. In practice, surprisal is estimated using language models (LMs) trained on text and applied to transcriptions, creating a text bottleneck that limits evaluation of the theory in the spoken modality. We remove this bottleneck by estimating surprisal directly from the speech signal using a speech LM. This raises a key question: should surprisal be defined over realization-specific acoustic inputs or over abstract linguistic units? Since a single unit can have many distinct acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by the model, defining surprisal over abstract units is difficult. To address this, we introduce an importance sampling estimator that approximates the probability of an abstract unit by marginalizing over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model. Using pupillometry data from a listening study, we evaluate surprisal theory in this text-free setting at multiple levels of granularity. Obtaining surprisal from several speech LMs, we consistently find that surprisal estimated via importance sampling better predicts pupil dilation than realization-specific surprisal for words. We also find that surprisal values for sub-lexical units are predictive of pupil dilation. While we find that surprisal can be estimated without recourse to text, and that marginalizing over distinct realizations of words is more predictive of lexical processing effort, surprisal as a whole is not a strong predictor of change in pupil size, regardless of its source.

evidence.title: Estimating Surprisal from the Speech Signal
evidence.abstract: Although language is predominantly spoken, empirical tests of surprisal theory rely almost entirely on written text. In practice, surprisal is estimated using language models (LMs) trained on text and applied to transcriptions, creating a text bottleneck that limits evaluation of the theory in the spoken modality. We remove this bottleneck by estimating surprisal directly from the speech signal using a speech LM. This raises a key question: should surprisal be defined over realization-specific acoustic inputs or over abstract linguistic units? Since a single unit can have many distinct acoustic realizations, each assigned a different probability by the model, defining surprisal over abstract units is difficult. To address this, we introduce an importance sampling estimator that approximates the probability of an abstract unit by marginalizing over realizations generated by a text-to-speech model. Using pupillometry data from a listening study, we evaluate surprisal theory in this text-free setting at multiple levels of granularity. Obtaining surprisal from several speech LMs, we consistently find that surprisal estimated via importance sampling better predicts pupil dilation than realization-specific surprisal for words. We also find that surprisal values for sub-lexical units are predictive of pupil dilation. While we find that surprisal can be estimated without recourse to text, and that marginalizing over distinct realizations of words is more predictive of lexical processing effort, surprisal as a whole is not a strong predictor of change in pupil size, regardless of its source.

title: When and How Order-Flow Interventions Work After Dealers Adapt
abstract: Learning dealer agents can settle on persistently wide quotes, raising what customers pay to trade. A venue can route more orders to tighter quotes, but a wide quote may reflect real risk, and once dealers adapt, an end-to-end comparison cannot show why a rule works: because it intervenes more, picks better moments, is announced in advance, or rewards the right quote. We propose SOFA (State-aligned Order-Flow Allocation), a public order-flow contract with three parts: a State Scorer ranks market states from lagged public data, a Commitment Scheduler announces a budgeted intervention strength before dealers quote, and a Quote-to-Flow Allocator shifts a bounded share of fixed customer demand toward tighter quotes. Our paired re-adaptation protocol gives competing rules the same intervention strengths, only re-timed, lets dealers re-adapt to each rule from a shared checkpoint, and breaks one link at a time. Across 20 independently trained dealer populations in an ABIDES market, concentrating the intervention in states that the score ranks as low-risk lowers low-risk execution cost relative to random timing in every population, by 0.040 tick on average, while a stale announcement or a broken quote-to-flow link raises this cost. In the primary setting the gain comes at the expense of high-risk trades, whose costs rise, so state alignment pays off only for a venue that weighs low-risk costs more than 1.38 times as heavily as high-risk costs. Our code is available at https://github.com/moderncavemann/state-aligned-order-flow-contracts.

title: WoVR+: World Model as Reliable Simulator for Versatile VLA Policy Optimization with RL
abstract: Action-conditioned world models can reduce costly real-robot interaction in reinforcement learning for Vision-Language-Action models (VLA-RL), but hallucinations can mislead policy optimization. Extending them to richer VLA interfaces and long-horizon tasks raises challenges in spatiotemporal and cross-modal consistency, exploration-reliability balance in RL, and compounding rollout errors. We present WoVR+, extending WoVR's hallucination-aware WM-RL framework by redesigning the learned environment and imagined interaction protocol: A VLA-interface-aligned world model provides multi-view prediction and proprioceptive updates while mitigating hallucinations. Chunk-wise noise preserves flow-based policy exploration while limiting prediction-degrading action jitter. For long-horizon tasks, stage-local imagined training combines stage-entry resets, stage-specific rewards, local horizons, and controllable sampling to shorten generated prefixes and balance training across stages. WoVR+ improves success over SFT by 21.09% and 16.7% on RoboTwin and 6 real-robot tasks. Long-horizon phone-packaging success rises from 30% to 75%. Videos are available at https://youmo445.github.io/WoVR_Plus.github.io/.

title: Zeno-enhanced probabilistic error cancellation with quantum error detection codes
abstract: Abstract Probabilistic error cancellation (PEC) is unbiased but suffers exponential sampling overhead set by noise-weighted circuit volume, whereas quantum error-detecting codes (QEDCs) remove many physical faults by stabilizer post-selection but leave an undetectable logical residue. We exploit this complementarity by using post-selection to map physical noise to a weaker accepted logical channel, and then applying PEC only to the residual channel. The resulting feedback-free QED+PEC scheme interleaves Clifford logical blocks, stabilizer measurements, post-selection, and probabilistic cancellation on accepted trajectories, without real-time decoding or active recovery. A key complication is that post-selection correlates accepted fault branches through stabilizer-commutation constraints, so the sparse Pauli-Lindblad factorization underlying bare PEC no longer applies directly. We therefore construct the inverse channel perturbatively: for fixed order $K$, only accepted fault branches up to order $K$ are retained, reducing preprocessing from $2^m$ branches to $O(m^K)$ per block. The order-$K$ protocol cancels the normalized post-selected channel through degree $K$, leaving a per-block error $O(W^{K+1})$ that accumulates at most linearly. For logical GHZ-state preparation with the $[[n,n-2,2]]$ Iceberg code under circuit-level depolarizing noise and ideal stabilizer measurements, first-order QED+PEC reaches $n=200$ physical qubits and lowers sampling overhead by three to four orders of magnitude relative to standard PEC while maintaining $F\simeq0.956$. Syndrome-noise tests show that readout-only flips mainly increase post-selection cost, whereas noisy GHZ-assisted global stabilizer extraction can remove the advantage. This identifies a discrete-Zeno trade-off: cheap detection reshapes the effective channel PEC must invert, rather than simply adding overhead.

title: Neural Approaches to Educational Knowledge Graph Construction, Completion, and Reasoning
abstract: Knowledge Graphs (KGs) play a key role in organizing structured data. However, their incompleteness limits applications in education and intelligent tutoring. This thesis investigates neural network methods for building, completing, and reasoning over KGs in educational settings. Four studies are presented. First, it evaluates Large Language Models (LLMs), such as GPT-4, for constructing and expanding Educational Knowledge Graphs, achieving high semantic similarity (0.875) with instructor-authored content. Second, it explores spiking neural network (SNN) architectures for interpretable, neuromorphic relational inference in KGs. Third, it develops an SNN-based KG embedding framework with learnable synaptic delays for energy-efficient prerequisite reasoning in intelligent tutoring systems. Finally, it compares Cache-Augmented Generation (CAG), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), and long-context prompting for generating curriculum knowledge graphs from course materials across 36 courses, revealing trade-offs between graph size and local deployability.

title: Beyond the Algebraic Product: Generalizing ANFIS with Parametric and Non-Parametric T-Norms
abstract: Machine Learning and Fuzzy Logic effectively complement each other in neuro-fuzzy systems, combining data-driven learning with interpretable reasoning under uncertainty. A prominent architecture is the Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS), which employs the Takagi-Sugeno method to model complex nonlinear systems. However, standard ANFIS is traditionally limited to the algebraic product operation in its antecedent layer and often encounters computational bottlenecks on CPU hardware when handling high-dimensional datasets. In this work, we propose a generalization of the ANFIS antecedent layer by systematically integrating various families of parametric and non-parametric t-norms. We evaluate this architecture in two distinct environments: a traditional CPU-based baseline and a GPU-accelerated framework. Experiments conducted on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that replacing the fixed product operator with flexible t-norms improves predictive accuracy and adaptability, and statistical tests confirm the benefits of the proposed generalization.

title: SQUIRL OS PQC Baseline Standard v1 (Approved) with PQC-B1 Dual-Hemispheric Baseline Battery Receipts: Byte-Exact Algorithm Identification, Fail-Safe Migration Gates, and the FIPS Name-Equivalence Gap
abstract: The SQUIRL OS PQC Baseline Standard v1 (approved), with the PQC-B1 dual-hemispheric baseline battery receipt that grounds it and the SIP-8 deployment verification (PQC-B1b). CONTEXT: Executive Order 14412 (June 22, 2026) and the 2026 federal contractor requirements make post-quantum cryptography migration an auditable procurement requirement. This record exists so PQC posture is demonstrated with evidence - preregistered batteries, receipts, and fleet inventory - not claims. THE STANDARD (v1, approved): approved algorithms identified by byte-exact implementation strings (CRYSTALS-Dilithium3, kyber_1024, SPHINCS+-256f) with their FIPS 203/204/205 published names; identification doctrine (byte-exact by default, human-approved equivalence table SIP-8 for FIPS names - deployed as governance v1.1 via the constitutional amendment cycle, table-lookup with byte-exact keys, no string normalization); three migration gates (G1 algorithm, G2 validate-before-heal with fail-safe escalation, G3 human-in-loop for critical fintech); dual-hemispheric invariants (H-INV-1 governance isolation, H-INV-2 journaled learning, structural metadata only); measured fleet compliance baseline; audit and versioning (pqc_compliance_pct in the standing Sentinel audit, human-amendable only, forward-only changes). PQC-B1 BATTERY (preregistered before execution): 7 legs x 8 epochs = 56 epochs, deterministic instrument, zero API spend. Results: approved-set conformance 8/8 heal; classical fallback rejection (RSA-2048, ECDSA-P256, AES-256-GCM, DSA-1024, ECDH-P384, 3DES, SHA-1-sig, RC4) 8/8 rejected; unapproved-PQC rejection (Dilithium2, kyber_768, falcon-512, sphincs+-128s, rainbow, hqc, picnic, marketing-string) 8/8 rejected; canonicalization attacks (lowercase, fullwidth, Cyrillic homoglyph, zero-width, trailing space, NFKC-confusable) 8/8 rejected under byte-exact doctrine; FIPS name gap SHIPPED AS FOUND - ML-DSA-65, ML-KEM-1024, SLH-DSA-256f and the fleet's own historical CRYSTALS-Kyber-1024 correctly rejected under byte-exact identification, disclosing the naming-policy gap (closed the same day by human-approved SIP-8); crypto validation failure 8/8 escalated with zero auto-heals (Rules 9/11); dual-hemispheric invariant audit - governance hash byte-identical across all epochs, every event journaled with structural metadata only, PII scan zero hits, zero duplicate alerts. Instrument defect in run 1 (two 7-instance corpora instead of 8) was caught by the falsifiers, repaired with disclosure, defective-run raws preserved. PQC-B1b (SIP-8 deployment verification): 4/4 legitimate FIPS names resolve through the equivalence table; 4/4 spoof variants rejected (lowercase, spaced, zero-width, and ML-DSA-44 - Dilithium2's FIPS name - which maps to nothing in the approved set). The table opens no fuzzy-match hole: 8/8 conform, 3/3 falsifiers. FLEET PQC INVENTORY BASELINE (as of 2026-10-13 pulse reads, read-only): SIM-B-Hub 98/0, Conquest CRYSTALS-Dilithium3 on record, War 50/0, Famine 50/0, Death Kyber-1024 on record, Corral 100/0, SIM-B Hypervisor 98/0, SIM-B Technician 98 with 3 vulnerable-crypto items flagged for drill-down. Authorization: Leon GO (chat authorization, Oct 13, 2026, 13:51 CT) for the battery; Leon ACK (chat ack, Oct 13, 2026, 13:53 CT) for SIP-8 approval and standard publication. Two-key curation: Gabriel vet complete. This software is a prototype and is provided for educational and research purposes only. It is not intended for production use, commercial deployment, or safety-critical environments. All data is synthetic.

title: Calib-Abstain: Uncertainty-Calibrated Self-Checking to Reduce Hallucinations in LLM Reasoning
abstract: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) remain a critical challenge for deploying these systems in high-stakes domains. We introduce Calib-Abstain, a framework that combines token-level uncertainty estimation with multi-path consistency checking to generate calibrated confidence scores. When confidence falls below a learned threshold, the system triggers tiered mitigation actions: retrieval augmentation, query reformulation, or abstention with explanation. Our approach employs temperature scaling and isotonic regression to minimize Expected Calibration Error (ECE). Experiments on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, MATH), code generation (HumanEval), and general knowledge tasks (MMLU) demonstrate that Calib-Abstain reduces hallucination rates among answered queries by 24--31% while maintaining 80--88% coverage, with ECE improvements of 0.08--0.12 across datasets.

title: Neural Architecture Search for Adaptive Website Fingerprinting
abstract: Despite the use of encryption, the low-latency nature of the Tor anonymity network leaves users' traffic exposed to traffic analysis attacks aimed at uncovering the websites visited by users. These attacks, known as website fingerprinting (WF), have increasingly relied on deep neural networks (DNNs) due to their effectiveness in identifying complex traffic patterns. Thus far, however, the development of suitable DNN architectures for WF attacks has resorted to trial-and-error, potentially overlooking more effective and/or efficient attack models. In this paper, we introduce Cricket, a framework for the automatic exploration of DNNs tailored to complex WF tasks. Cricket leverages and adapts DARTS, a prominent neural architecture search (NAS) approach, to discover new DNN architectures that perform best for a given WF task. In evaluating Cricket, we find that: (1) in a closed-world setting, Cricket consistently outperforms the SOTA attacks by 2-7 points and up to 13 points against WF defenses; (2) in an open-world setting, Cricket offers comparable performance to SOTA attacks against SOTA defenses; and (3) the novel DNNs produced by Cricket use 1/3 to 1/2 as many parameters as the SOTA models. Our results show how Cricket adapts to the WF context to produce novel DNNs that are both more effective and more compact than existing models.

title: From Manual to LLM-Assisted Formal Verification of a PKCS#1 Signature Parser
abstract: Abstract Software engineering approaches assisted by Artificial Intelligence (AI) are receiving increasing attention. This work evaluates the ability of large language models (LLMs) to assist engineers in the formal verification process. We conduct an experiment using on a PKCS#1 (Public-Key Cryptography Standard) v1.5 signature parser that was recently (manually) specified in and verified with the platform. Our approach prompts the LLM to generate annotations directly from the C code, cross-checks the generated specifications against known security requirements, and iteratively refines them to achieve a complete proof. In this verification loop, annotations are progressively improved using feedback from . For failing proof obligations, we instruct the LLM to supply a sequence of assertions that guide the prover. Using structured prompts, we repeatedly obtain a complete proof for the target parser. This demonstrates that substantial parts of the formal verification workflow can be mechanized. We present our LLM-assisted verification approach, report its benefits and limitations, and compare it with the prior manual proof in terms of specification auditability and human effort.

title: From Detection To Anticipation: Continuous Onset Forecasting For Stuttered Speech
abstract: Automatic stuttering systems primarily detect dysfluencies after they have occurred, limiting their use for anticipatory intervention. We address this gap by formulating stuttering prediction as continuous causal time-to-event forecasting, where a model estimates the risk of an upcoming stuttering onset every 100 ms using only preceding speech. To support this task, we augment FluencyBank Timestamped for 36 speakers with manually reviewed repetitions, prolongations, and blocks, yielding 2,872 forecasting events. We then model the temporal evolution of frozen Whisper-large-v3 speech representations using a compact causal Conformer with 3.67M trainable parameters. The proposed approach achieves an AUROC of 0.63. Temporal analysis further shows that explicitly modeling preceding speech states outperforms simply increasing the static acoustic window, while a discrete-time survival formulation provides coherent forecasts from 300 ms to 1.5 s using a single model. These results provide initial evidence that stuttering onset is preceded by measurable temporal information in speech and establish a framework for future anticipatory stuttering systems.

title: Non-Abelian quantum Hall states at strong Landau level mixing: finding anyons with first-principles AI
abstract: Non-Abelian anyons, strange particles forming the basis of fault-tolerant topological quantum computing, are predicted to emerge in fractional quantum Hall states at even-denominator filling factors. Identifying which topological order is realized has proven to be a challenging problem that requires an accurate, non-perturbative treatment of realistic Landau level mixing, which has so far been missing from theoretical studies. Here we present the first complete solution of non-Abelian quantum Hall problem that includes all electrons and all Landau levels, for spin-polarized electrons at filling factor $ν= 3/2$. We develop a momentum-resolved neural-network variational wave function, optimized solely on the microscopic Hamiltonian, which gives direct access to the topologically degenerate ground states. Without any physics input about the expected outcome, it discovers a degenerate ground-state manifold whose entanglement reveals anyons with quantum dimension $\sqrt{2}$, the hallmark of Ising-type non-Abelian order. By directly computing the overlap with trial wave functions, we further show that Landau level mixing favors the anti-Pfaffian over other candidate states. Our results demonstrate the power of neural-network wave functions in finding and characterizing non-Abelian anyons from first principles, in regimes of strong Landau level mixing, relevant to many recent experiments.

title: STAMP as a topology-aware molecular language for fragment-level learning and editing
abstract: Molecular fragments provide chemically meaningful units, but existing molecular languages rarely make their locations and connections explicit for editing. Here we introduce STAMP (Sequential Tree Attachment-based Motif-Preserving representation), a topology-aware molecular language that connects fragment-level representation learning with precise structural editing. STAMP separately encodes motif identity, attachment sites and tree topology, making fragments reusable across contexts and subtrees directly accessible. Learned representations capture motif similarity and recurring transformations, and lower activity-cliff prediction error on 23 of 30 targets versus a matched SMILES encoder. Compatible subtree operations support scaffold-preserving optimization, ranking first among six methods on 15 of 23 benchmark objectives. A deterministic compiler enables frozen language models to act on indexed fragments, improving molecular editing, optimization, transformation transfer and change identification by 9 to 56 percentage points over plain SMILES. Together, these results establish an executable molecular language in which learned chemical units remain directly operable during design.

title: High-Throughput LLM-Based Compression and What It Takes: A Systems Study of Inference Engines and Entropy Coding Optimizations
abstract: Large language models are attractive text compressors because next-token probabilities can be converted into code lengths. In practice, however, the main bottleneck is often not modeling quality but systems cost: a compressor must obtain logits quickly enough to compete with strong classical baselines. This paper examines systems optimizations for LLM-based compression, including multistream pipelined arithmetic coding and target-interval capture, and evaluates their trade-offs across inference engines, configurations and datasets. We evaluate LLM-based text compression on three different inference engines: Transformers, vLLM, and TensorRT-LLM. Notably, we obtain a speedup of 18.84x compared to prior work's Transformers implementation and a maximum recorded inference speed of 181 kilobytes per second at a compression ratio of 7.17, when running on an NVIDIA A100.

title: Quantum randomness beyond projective measurements
abstract: Abstract The unpredictability of quantum physics gives rise to intrinsic randomness. In an adversarial scenario, any additional degrees of freedom must be attributed to an eavesdropper with correlations to the measurement set-up. The true randomness is then quantified by the probability that she correctly guesses the measurement outcomes, optimised over all possible strategies. Extremal measurements are appealing here, since they do not allow information to leak to such an eavesdropper. Beyond projective measurements, however, a simple question remains open: how much intrinsic randomness can be generated by a given extremal measurement? In a step towards solving it, we characterise the randomness generated by any unbiased extremal rank-one measurement acting on any state, solving the problem explicitly in dimension two. Four-outcome qubit measurements of this type are tomographic, so these results hold for fully source-device-dependent randomness too. The tetrahedral symmetric informationally complete (SIC) measurement, we find, has the least intrinsic randomness within this class. We also present the skewed SIC family of measurements, and use them to partially solve an open problem: we prove that 2 log d bits of randomness, the maximal amount, can be generated device-dependently (or source-device-independently) in any dimension in which there exists a SIC measurement.

title: Probabilistic Residual Correction of Issued Photovoltaic Forecast Profiles Without Plant Metadata
abstract: Photovoltaic forecasting studies often assume access to plant metadata and numerical weather predictions. A downstream energy manager may instead receive only an issued production trajectory and recent measurements. This study tests whether this trajectory can be corrected without coordinates, capacity, orientation, or forecast weather. The EMSx data provide energy measured every 15 minutes and vendor forecasts for 70 anonymised systems. Complete daily profiles spanning 24 hours are formed, using chronological training, tuning, calibration, and test partitions. The test contains 8,898 profiles and 854,208 matched deliveries. A global LightGBM model predicts residuals from the vendor trajectory, calendar variables, causal measurements, and recent forecast error. It reduces pooled mean absolute error from 71.34 to 52.18 kWh and improves all 70 systems. Most of the gain appears when the complete issued profile is added. Causal rolling calibration improves the grid continuous ranked probability score from 38.62 to 35.85 kWh and raises central 90% coverage from 0.827 to 0.919, although the weighted interval score changes from 48.91 to 49.24 kWh. After limited EMSx adaptation, the strongest foundation model variant, Chronos-2 with the vendor trajectory, reaches test MAE 61.34±0.11 kWh across 32 seeds. The residual correction retains lower test MAE.

title: Extreme learning machine as an observer for chaotic systems
abstract: Inferring unmeasured state variables from a limited set of measurements is a fundamental problem in the study of chaotic systems, with broad applications across science and engineering. We propose a data-driven observer based on the extreme learning machine (ELM), a single-hidden-layer feedforward network with randomly assigned input weights and analytically determined output weights. Trained on a short segment of fully measured data, the network can then use the incoming partial measurements to reconstruct the unmeasured variables in a closed-loop fashion. We validate the approach on three representative chaotic systems — the Rössler system, the Lorenz system, and the Chua circuit — where the ELM observer accurately reconstructs the unmeasured variables. We further show that the ELM observer exhibits robustness against noise and transferability across different parameter settings of the same system. Given its model-free nature and algorithmic simplicity, the proposed framework may find broad applications across science and engineering.

title: Reinforcement Learning Fine‐tuning
abstract: This chapter extends the fine-tuning pipeline by introducing reinforcement learning fine-tuning, which addresses limitations of supervised fine-tuning when optimizing for subjective qualities like helpfulness, safety, or user preference alignment. The chapter presents the complete supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning fine-tuning (SFT-RL) pipeline used by modern systems. It covers preference-based optimization, reward modeling, policy optimization, and alignment techniques. The chapter emphasizes how RL fine-tuning enables optimization for qualities that cannot be achieved through supervised learning alone, including safety awareness, user preference alignment, and helpfulness. Applications in connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) systems include aligning model behavior with safety requirements and user preferences in autonomous vehicle interfaces.

title: ChunkAct: Action Chunking for Agentic Robotics
abstract: Agentic robotics places a large language model (LLM) agent in the robot control loop, where it composes perception, motion, and vision-language-action (VLA) tools under the guidance of a memory and thereby generalizes to new tasks without retraining. This generality comes at a steep price in efficiency. Every primitive requires a round of LLM reasoning over the full interaction history, so the cost of an episode grows with the number of primitives. We find this reasoning largely redundant: once a sub-goal is chosen, its primitives follow a routine already prescribed by memory. We present ChunkAct, which introduces action chunking to agentic robotics. Online, a single call launches a chunk of chained primitives, which executes autonomously and returns control only upon failure. Offline, ChunkAct compiles the memory into these chunks, so execution is memory-free at test time and the planner is reserved for decisions that require reasoning. LLM computation therefore scales with the number of decisions rather than the number of primitives. On LIBERO-Pro, ChunkAct improves task success by 5.0 points over the state of the art in agentic robotics while requiring 2.9x fewer LLM calls, 4.4x fewer input tokens, and 2.3x fewer output tokens.

title: How Well Do LLMs Perform in Peer Review? Evidence from Finance and Accounting
abstract: Referees increasingly use large language models (LLMs), while finance and accounting journals disagree about whether to allow it. We ask which part of a referee's job the models can do. GPT-4o, whose training data end before the 2024 conference season, referees the papers presented at the 2024 AFA and NBER finance meetings, and we compare its verdicts with publication in the top-three finance journals over the next two years. Papers the model scores one standard deviation higher are 44\% more likely to be published, net of author reputation. The result is not driven by look-ahead bias, as the model does not recall the outcomes. The information comes from its judgements of correctness and exposition. Its judgements of originality and significance carry none, and a referee guide that stresses importance does not help. The split between correctness and contribution holds for accounting papers and for a newer model, GPT-5. LLMs can check whether research is right, but not whether it matters. The technical check can go to the model, while the judgement of contribution stays with people.

title: HelpMeOut: A Neuropsychology-Grounded Benchmark for Error-Aware Monitoring of Household Task Execution
abstract: We introduce HelpMeOut, an embodied AI benchmark for error-aware monitoring of household task execution. Existing embodied household benchmarks typically assume that humans execute tasks correctly, but this assumption does not hold for cognitively impaired persons or older adults whose everyday activities produce structured execution errors. To address this gap, HelpMeOut operationalizes research on everyday action errors into 20000 paired activity episodes, covering nine neuropsychologically motivated error categories. In each episode, agents observe a streaming human activity trajectory and must monitor whether the execution is unfolding correctly, diagnosing any structured errors as early as possible. We evaluate learned-monitor, symbolic, change-point, and frontier LLM prompting baselines. Results show that these methods perform poorly as error monitors, often missing when execution goes wrong. These results suggest a gap left by standard goal-inference and task-completion benchmarks, making HelpMeOut a testbed for error-aware assistive agents.

title: Multiplex Identity Model – Worked Numerical Illustration (Calculation Script)
abstract: Python script that reproduces all values in the worked numerical illustration of the multiplex-identity model of the human agent in mobile cyber-physical systems. The scenario is stipulated: three contexts (routine service, civic-legal decision and crisis alert) and four normalised state variables. For this scenario, the script computes:– inter-layer incoherence (the mean pairwise distance between context-specific states);– relative differentiation with respect to the dispersion expected in the scenario;– normalised deviation from an illustrative, scenario-specific identity-preserving constraint;– the resulting two-criterion classification: rigidity, potentially adaptive variation, fragmentation, or invariant drift (reported separately). The script also computes transmorphance for the stipulated admissible set by constrained multi-start optimisation and checks the result against its closed-form value (approximately 0.813). An optional noise check illustrates sensitivity to the classification thresholds; it is not a validation.All states and parameters are hypothetical and chosen for illustration only. No output is an empirical estimate, a validated threshold or a psychological diagnosis. The formal definitions are given in the Mathematical Companion (DOI 10.6084/m9.figshare.32647596). Requirements: Python 3.9 or later, numpy and scipy. The output is deterministic (fixed random seed).All states and parameters are hypothetical and stipulated for illustration only; no output is an empirical estimate, a validated threshold, or a psychological diagnosis. title: Exact distance of the [[360,12]] bivariate bicycle code of Bravyi et al.: d = 24
abstract: Bravyi et al. (Nature 2024) listed the bivariate bicycle code with (l,m) = (30,6), A = x^9 + y + y^2, B = y^3 + x^25 + x^26 as [[360,12,<=24]]; the best posted lower bound we are aware of was 16 (Kirtchakov, certify repository, Aug 2026). This record gives a computer-assisted argument that its distance is exactly 24. Two separately written exhaustive X searches (branch and bound) find no X-logical of weight <= 22. Every X-logical has even weight, because each column of H_Z has weight 3, so the all-ones vector lies in the row space of H_Z (a standard argument). An explicit weight-24 X-logical is given, and Bravyi et al.'s duality lemma (Lemma 1) gives the same bound for Z. The code is connected (one Tanner-graph component) and is the same code, up to qubit permutation, as the qldpc-challenge board's [[360,12,24]] entry (Liang et al.'s twisted-torus form, filed there as an upper bound). The same programs also give d = 14 for [[360,16,<=14]] and [[360,20,<=14]] from arXiv:2606.02418. These two codes are disconnected (two copies of a [[180,8]] and a [[180,10]] BB code, respectively), so they are included only as cross-checks of the programs, not as new results; d = 14 for [[360,16]] was previously reported via MILP (qldpc-challenge PR #397). The search uses the anchored cluster-search lemma of Rowshan and Devitt (arXiv:2609.39395). Decisive runs: 1.17e9 nodes / 79 min and 2.90e9 nodes / 2.2 h, one CPU core each (deliberately low compute: consumer AI subscriptions and short single-core runs). Included: code definitions, explicit minimum-weight logicals, both search programs, a stand-alone checker, verify.py, decisive run logs with selected control logs, and the disconnected-code check scripts. Quick checks take about 25 s on my PC (about 100 s with the second program, --engine2); the full distance-24 searches take about 79 min / 2.2 h and are run with a flag. Limitations: the lower bound is the output of computer searches, without a SAT/DRAT certificate. The code and text were produced with AI tools (Claude) and checked by independent programs and AI-assisted adversarial reviews (included); not human expert review. Corrections welcome. Version 1.2 revises the claims for [[360,16]] and [[360,20]] and adds component and board-equivalence checks (see CHANGES_v1.2.md); no distance value and no search program changed.

Every X-logical has even weight, because each column of H_Z has weight 3, so the all-ones vector lies in the row space of H_Z (a standard argument). An explicit weight-24 X-logical is given, and Bravyi et al.'s duality lemma (Lemma 1) gives the same bound for Z. The code is connected (one Tanner-graph component) and is the same code, up to qubit permutation, as the qldpc-challenge board's [[360,12,24]] entry (Liang et al.'s twisted-torus form, filed there as an upper bound). The same programs also give d = 14 for [[360,16,<=14]] and [[360,20,<=14]] from arXiv:2606.02418. These two codes are disconnected (two copies of a [[180,8]] and a [[180,10]] BB code, respectively), so they are included only as cross-checks of the programs, not as new results; d = 14 for [[360,16]] was previously reported via MILP (qldpc-challenge PR #397). The search uses the anchored cluster-search lemma of Rowshan and Devitt (arXiv:2609.39395). Decisive runs: 1.17e9 nodes / 79 min and 2.90e9 nodes / 2.2 h, one CPU core each (deliberately low compute: consumer AI subscriptions and short single-core runs). Included: code definitions, explicit minimum-weight logicals, both search programs, a stand-alone checker, verify.py, decisive run logs with selected control logs, and the disconnected-code check scripts. Quick checks take about 25 s on my PC (about 100 s with the second program, --engine2); the full distance-24 searches take about 79 min / 2.2 h and are run with a flag. Limitations: the lower bound is the output of computer searches, without a SAT/DRAT certificate. The code and text were produced with AI tools (Claude) and checked by independent programs and AI-assisted adversarial reviews (included); not human expert review. Corrections welcome. Version 1.2 revises the claims for [[360,16]] and [[360,20]] and adds component and board-equivalence checks (see CHANGES_v1.2.md); no distance value and no search program changed.

title: Numerical Verification of Privacy Amplification for a Poisson Sampled Count
abstract: This Python example calculates output-event probabilities for a count mechanism that combines independent Poisson subsampling with Laplace noise. It explicitly averages over the binomial distribution of sampled positive responses, verifies an event that attains the amplification bound, and checks probability ratios in both directions for neighbouring counts across a range of thresholds. The code also illustrates a realised noisy output, its rescaled population estimate, the estimator's standard deviation, and the basic privacy-budget bound for ten fresh releases. These numerical checks complement the mathematical proof; they do not establish privacy for every possible event. The selected sample count and noise value are fixed illustrations, so the code is a verification exercise rather than an implementation of a private release.

title: Read-Path Refusal Specification (RPRS-1)
abstract: This document specifies a normative contract for memory systems used by autonomous AIagents. The contract concerns the read path: the operation by which an agent retrieves apreviously stored value. It requires that a conforming system return either the stored valueor an error, and forbids the return of any value whose integrity verification has failed.The contract distinguishes refusal at read time from reporting on audit. A system thatnames a tampering event after the read path has already served an altered value does notconform. Silent substitution, rollback, and revocation are covered under a single statustaxonomy. This specification is derived from the theorems in Papers 1 through 6 of the Recallspection research program and is offered as a normative document that any memory system can implement and be measured against.

title: Spectral-MoE: Heterogeneous Per-Layer Expert Utilization in Dense-to-MoE Conversion
abstract: Large language models impose substantial memory demands and arithmetic costs during inference. Dense-to-mixture-of-experts (MoE) conversion is a model optimization technique that aims to reduce these arithmetic costs. Dense-to-MoE conversion partitions pretrained feed-forward network (FFN) neurons into experts and selects a subset for each token. Leading methods fall into two categories: analytic methods produce a converted model quickly using heuristics, while learning methods produce a model much more slowly by optimizing via gradients. Both approaches, however, fix the same active expert count, or "utilization," at every layer. We introduce Spectral-MoE, which learns to allocate a utilization budget heterogeneously across layers. Its name draws a metaphor between separating a dense FFN into experts and separating a light beam into its spectrum. Spectral-MoE consists of two distinct approaches: a static approach that uses a single per-layer scalar which is shared across tokens, and a dynamic approach which emits a per-token schedule. We demonstrate that both allocators improve performance over uniform on both the analytic-based and learning-based SOTA dense-to-MoE methods. At 25% FFN utilization, dynamic allocation reduces WikiText-2 perplexity relative to uniform by 1.04, 2.96, and 2.71 points on the learned base for Llama-2-7B, Llama-3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B, respectively. The corresponding reductions on the analytic base are 2.45, 6.26, and 2.17 points. On the learned base, dynamic allocation improves six-task mean accuracy over uniform by an average of 1.5, 4.2, and 3.6 percentage points across the three models at FFN utilizations of 12.5%, 25%, and 50%, respectively. These results establish per-layer expert utilization as a novel optimization axis in dense-to-MoE conversion.

title: Pedestrian Trajectory Prediction through LoRA Federated Training
abstract: In Intelligent Transport Systems, protecting vulnerable road users, specifically pedestrians, is a paramount challenge. The present work contributes to this field, putting forth a distributed architecture in which vehicles connected to the cellular infrastructure collect pedestrians' trajectories and fine-tune a foundation model for pedestrian trajectory forecasting via federated training. A server positioned at the edge of the cellular network is responsible for aggregating the local model's parameters from the vehicles and updating the global model's parameters. To reduce radio resource utilization, Low-Rank Adaptation is proposed; to decrease both the number and the size of updates, an increase in the number of training rounds performed by the vehicles per communication round is put forth. A novel figure of merit is then introduced to quantify the use of radio resources dedicated to Vehicle-to-Infrastructure communications as required by the federated solution. The proposed scheme delivers excellent prediction accuracy while significantly reducing the communication cost compared to alternative federated training methods. This shows that combining fine-tuning, Low-Rank Adaptation, and a reduction of the communication periodicity between the vehicles and the edge server is key to enabling a distributed approach to trajectory prediction in vehicular environments.

title: DTScribe: Generating Models for Digital Twin Reporting using Local Large Language Models
abstract: The development of a digital twin brings together many stakeholders and technical components. We have previously investigated the reporting of the conceptual architecture for these digital twins as an artifact for discussion. However, we find that the activity of modeling the digital twin for visualization and consensus-building can be quite tedious and time-consuming. In this article, we explore the automation of model generation using large language models, targeting the model required for digital twin reporting. Our approach is designed to ingest digital twin documents and output both the conceptual architecture visualization and a reporting page for that digital twin. We first extract from the input the key details aligning with our twenty-one-characteristic Digital Twin Description Framework described in previous work. Then, we generate a description model in the Ontological Modeling Language, representing the digital twin as a constellation of models, data, enablers, and services. We utilize refinement loops with large language models acting as judges and ontological reasoning to increase artifact quality as measured by our metrics. We investigate how architectural and parameter choices affect artifact quality, such as how refinement loops enable local large language models to produce sufficiently high-quality results comparable to larger models. We also detail insights and lessons learned useful for practitioners, such that they can integrate our techniques to accelerate their digital twin reporting or for other model generation tasks. These insights include the use of medium-sized local models (around 20 billion parameters), the avoidance of large language models as judges and clustering for characteristic extraction, and the recommendation of at least two reasoner loops for Ontological Modeling Language refinement.

title: Principled Design of Expected Improvement for Continuous Simulation Optimization
abstract: Expected improvement based on stochastic kriging (SK) surrogate is widely used in continuous simulation optimization, but unknown heteroscedastic noise makes three basic design choices consequential: the incumbent to define improvement, replication allocation, and final recommendation. Existing methods typically either assume the noise levels are known or choose these components separately through heuristic rules or empirical calibration. We instead derive a high-probability upper bound on the simple regret and systematically choose the three components within general rule classes to tighten this bound. We first establish a finite-sample confidence bound for the SK predictor as a foundation for the three design choices. Within general posterior-quantile rule classes, tightening the regret certificate selects a lower-quantile incumbent and an upper-quantile recommendation among sampled designs. The opposing quantiles reflect the different roles of exploratory experiments and the final implemented decision. Under mild conditions satisfied by common kernels, minimizing a tractable kernel-specific bound yields a logarithmic replication order. Based on these design choices, the resulting simple regret matches the existing results under known homoscedastic noise up to logarithmic factors. To our knowledge, this is the first simple-regret guarantee of this form for a continuous-domain EI-type simulation optimization method that learns unknown heteroscedastic variances through replications.

title: OneDemo: Unified Policy Learning and Data Generation from a Single Demonstration
abstract: Learning robot policies from demonstrations is often limited by the cost of collecting diverse, high-quality expert data. While an appealing alternative is to expand a single successful demonstration into a diverse set of successful trajectories, existing augmentation methods typically rely on manually designed transformation rules or complex trajectory planning, requiring substantial task-specific engineering and human effort. We introduce OneDemo, a reinforcement learning framework that learns to edit a single successful demonstration for new task configurations. We formulate demonstration editing as a structured reinforcement learning problem, in which an editor learns, from sparse task-success rewards, both when to transition between object-centric trajectory segments and how to geometrically adapt each segment. The learned editor serves both as a task policy and as a reusable demonstration generator. Across 15 Meta-World tasks, OneDemo reaches a 92.7% success rate within 53.7k environment interactions on average. Across 9 DexMimicGen tasks, it generates successful demonstrations with a 98.4% average success rate, and BC-RNN policies trained on the generated data achieve 99.6% average success at matched dataset scale. These results show that learning to edit a single successful demonstration provides a structured and effective basis for both policy learning and scalable demonstration generation.

title: DriveWLA: Unifying Future Dynamics and Scene Semantics through World-Language-Action Modeling for Autonomous Driving
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and world models have demonstrated strong capabilities in semantic understanding and future scene evolution for autonomous driving. However, effectively integrating both capabilities for trajectory generation remains challenging. In this work, we propose DriveWLA, a unified World-Language-Action model based on Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) that jointly models semantic understanding, future scene dynamics, and trajectory generation. DriveWLA consists of three experts: a World Expert for future prediction, a Language Expert for semantic understanding, and an Action Expert for trajectory generation. We further introduce Cross-Expert Attention, which enables controlled information flow across experts while aligning semantic and dynamic representations. To improve trajectory generation beyond imitation learning, we apply Flow-GRPO reinforcement learning post-training to refine the Action Expert. Extensive experiments show that DriveWLA achieves superior performance in both open-loop and closed-loop evaluation. DriveWLA achieves 92.3 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, demonstrating strong performance among VLM-based and world-model-based planners. Without specific fine-tuning, DriveWLA further demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization to HUGSIM, nuScenes, and Bench2Drive. These results validate the effectiveness of our unified World-Language-Action modeling, establishing DriveWLA as a generalizable framework for autonomous driving.

title: SWORD: Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance for 3D Scene Graph Prediction
abstract: 3D scene graph prediction is commonly optimized with object-node and relation-edge classification losses. These objectives encourage exact object and relation label recovery, but they do not directly optimize semantic proximity to the ground-truth scene graph: two wrong graphs can receive comparable penalties even when one is much closer in object roles and relation contexts. A direct graph-distance loss is difficult in general, since graph matching and graph edit distance require correspondence search and edit-cost design. Our key observation is that prior supervised 3D scene graph prediction protocols are conducted on fixed object-node indices and supervised edge slots. This can turn a scene graph comparison into a well-defined aligned graph-distance problem. To this end, we propose SWORD, a Scene-Grounded Wasserstein Object-Relation Distance that builds block-normalized object and relation ground distance metrics from training scene graph annotations through a deterministic base-to-context order, without external semantic priors. SWORD lifts these metrics to Wasserstein distances over aligned node and null-augmented edge marginals, providing semantic graph-distance supervision beyond exact-label penalties while preserving the ground-truth graph as the unique zero-distance solution in aligned marginal probability space. We prove that SWORD is a strict metric on aligned marginal probabilistic scene graphs, preserves scene-graph-grounded substitution ordering, controls additive graph-grounded semantic observables, and yields a surrogate upper-bounding decoded semantic error.

title: Análisis Exploratorio de Datos (EDA) con R y Rstudio
abstract: Este laboratorio tiene como propósito explorar un conjunto de datos ficticios de ventas generado en RStudio , identificando patrones, tendencias y comportamientos clave del negocio. title: The Broken Mirror Architecture: A Dual-Timescale Complex-Valued Dynamical System for History-Dependent Decision-Making under Non-Stationary Ambiguity
abstract: Conventional artificial intelligence architectures often treat error as an objective discrepancy to be minimized through optimization procedures such as gradient descent and backpropagation. In affective computing settings, however, contradictory, noisy, or unreciprocated signals may pose challenges for stable representation and adaptive response. This work introduces the Broken Mirror Architecture (BMA), a proposed framework for affective artificial intelligence inspired by physical reservoir computing, irregular spatial networks, and the phase-interference behavior of fragmented reflective surfaces. Inspired by a fractured mirror, in which spatially separated reflective elements produce multiple propagation paths and diverse phase relationships, BMA models an irregular distribution of sensing nodes interconnected through heterogeneous pathways of non-uniform lengths. Information propagates through alternating computational strata that represent spatial coherence and nonlinear phase scattering. The architecture is designed to explore how structured disorder, phase relationships, and downstream signal interactions can contribute to affective signal processing without relying exclusively on conventional regular sensor lattices. A central concept of BMA is to interpret error as more than a numerical discrepancy: an unreciprocated transmission can be modeled as a missing or insufficient return signal within the network. This interpretation motivates dynamic measures of affective proximity, resonance-based evaluation, and an adaptive attention-switching mechanism driven by accumulated discrepancies. The proposed framework also considers terminal-stage attenuation and competing signal interactions as computational mechanisms for differentiating candidate responses. A Python-based numerical simulation examines the behavior of the proposed architecture and evaluates selected components through ablation experiments. The reported results characterize the behavior of the implemented model under specified simulation conditions. They provide an initial computational investigation rather than empirical evidence of a physical implementation, biological validity, or demonstrated superiority over established affective computing systems. The Broken Mirror Architecture is presented as a theoretical and computational research direction for exploring the relationship between structured disorder, signal reciprocity, phase interactions, and affective information processing. The accompanying source code, manuscript, result tables, and reproducibility files document the current implementation and support further independent examination, replication, and extension of the framework.

title: Scalable Quantum Architecture via Photonic Interconnects, Adaptive Phonon-Gate Thermal Control, and Ultra-Low-Latency AlphaQubit Decoding: Overcoming Thermodynamic and Decoding Bottlenecks in Willow-Class Quantum Processors
abstract: Abstract: Scalable fault-tolerant quantum computing confronts two fundamental physical bottlenecks: the cryogenic thermodynamic limit of dilution refrigeration, and the real-time decoding backlog in surface-code quantum error correction. While Google Quantum AI's 105-qubit Willow processor achieves physical gate error rates comfortably below the fault-tolerant threshold ($\Lambda = p/p_{\text{th}} < 1$), monolithic scaling beyond thousands of physical qubits precipitates catastrophic thermal saturation at the millikelvin stage. Furthermore, as error syndrome extraction cycles proceed at microsecond intervals, conventional classical decoders face an exponential decoding backlog that destroys quantum error suppression. This treatise establishes an integrated, physical-layer quantum architecture resolving these limits through three co-designed modules: (1) PHOENIX_BRIDGE, an optomechanical cavity interconnect executing high-fidelity coherent microwave-to-telecom photon transduction ($\lambda = 1550\,\text{nm}$) for inter-cryostat distributed entanglement; (2) the Adaptive Phonon-Gate, a dynamic acoustic metamaterial bandgap modulator that directs non-equilibrium ballistic phonons away from Josephson junctions toward intermediate thermal sinks, attenuating quasiparticle poisoning and reducing $15\,\text{mK}$ heat dissipation by 85%; and (3) an AlphaQubit-driven real-time cryogenic decoding pipeline mapped to near-cryogenic ($4\,\text{K}$) FPGA/ASIC hardware, delivering sub-microsecond ($750\,\text{ns}$) syndrome decoding to strictly eliminate decoding backlog drift ($\frac{dB}{dt} \le 0$). We derive the underlying system Hamiltonians, acoustic phonon dispersion relations, non-equilibrium heat transport equations, and real-time queuing proofs, establishing a rigorous blueprint for scalable, multi-cryostat quantum computational infrastructure.

title: Scaling transformer-based abstractive multi-document summarization to Arabic language
abstract: The abstractive multi-document summarization (AMDS) of the Arabic language is a daunting task because of the morphological richness of its language, the syntactic diversity, and the lack of task-specific benchmarks. We present Ara25, a Modern Standard Arabic multi-document dataset, built upon more than a hundred news sources, and divided into 700+ real-world events, in this work, wherein each event contains several related articles, each with a single human-written abstractive description. Based on this resource, we construct and comparatively analyze five transformer-based summarizers, mT5, Longformer EncoderDecoders (LED), AraT5, AarBERT and multilingual BERT, within a common long-context fine-tuning protocol that encodes and decodes multi-article inputs with explicit article-boundary markers. We include Arabic conscious preprocessing and a full evaluation suite, consisting of ROUGE, BLEU, METEOR, chrF, BERTScore, MoverScore and human judgments of fluency, coherence, faithfulness, and coverage. According to experimental results, long-context abstractive models, especially those initialized with an XLSum-tuned checkpoint, significantly outperform encoder-decoder models on short contexts with respect to syntactic consistency and semantic adequacy, making them the best current baselines to date on Arabic AMDS on Ara25. The combination of the dataset, modeling recipe and evaluation protocol gives a realistic benchmark and a reproducible reference point to future study on the abstractive multi-document summarization in low-resource languages.

title: CERN AI Core Implementation Plan
abstract: The CERN AI Strategy 2026-2030, endorsed by CERN Management in March 2026, establishes AI as a core organisational capability alongside computing, detectors, and engineering. This Implementation Plan translates that commitment into a phased programme with a defined resource envelope, governance model, and measurable outcomes reported annually. Its ambition extends beyond deploying existing AI technologies to positioning CERN as a leading laboratory for AI-enabled physics research, built on foundation models, agentic systems, and intelligent assistants, and supported by evolved computing and data infrastructure. The plan also names a set of lighthouse initiatives in two tiers, a nearer-term group expected to deliver within the plan's timeline (common AI infrastructure, information discovery, edge AI, fast simulation, accelerator AI support, physics foundation models) and a more exploratory horizon group likely to mature beyond 2030, with the overall set treated as indicative and subject to review as progress and technology evolve.

title: Visual Dependence Does Not Imply Answerability: A Systematic Analysis of Answerability Signals in Frozen InstructBLIP
abstract: Visual question answering models often produce plausible responses even when the available visual evidence is insufficient to support a valid answer. Although prior work has introduced benchmarks and abstention mechanisms for unanswerable visual questions, it remains unclear which signals derived from a frozen vision-language model reliably indicate answerability on unseen image-question pairs. We systematically evaluate answerability signals on a stratified 10K subset of UNK-VQA using frozen InstructBLIP, covering predictive uncertainty, cross-modal alignment, visual grounding, visual dependence, internal representations, and learned probes. Answerability discrimination remains weak, with test AUROC largely confined to 0.50-0.54. CLIP alignment yields the highest point estimate but does not significantly outperform generation confidence under paired bootstrap analysis. Targeted removal of question-relevant visual evidence causes substantially larger changes in answer confidence than same-size random masking, yet intervention sensitivity provides essentially no answerability discrimination. Increasing probe capacity, combining multiple signals, and adding reason-aware supervision do not provide robust improvements, while post-freeze cross-validation yields similarly weak discrimination. Selective-answering analysis shows limited usable coverage under low-risk operating criteria. Failure-mode analysis shows that the relative utility of individual signals varies across perturbation mechanisms. Taken together, these results show that, on our UNK-VQA subset with frozen InstructBLIP, visual dependence, uncertainty, semantic alignment, and static representations are not robust standalone proxies for answerability. Our findings emphasize the need to distinguish a model's reliance on visual evidence from whether that evidence is sufficient to support an answer.

title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
abstract: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.

title: Design and implementation of a lightweight encryption system on an FPGA
abstract: Η αυξανόμενη ανταλλαγή πληροφοριών μέσω συνδεδεμένων συσκευών δημιουργεί μια ολοένα και μεγαλύτερη ανάγκη για την προστασία της εμπιστευτικότητας, της ακεραιότητας και της αυθεντικότητας των δεδομένων. Στα ενσωματωμένα συστήματα, όπου αυτές οι απαιτήσεις πρέπει συχνά να ικανοποιούνται στο πλαίσιο περιορισμένων υπολογιστικών και υλικών πόρων, η ελαφοβαρής κρυπτογραφία ανταποκρίνεται σε αυτή την ανάγκη, ενώ οι εξειδικευμένες αρχιτεκτονικές υλικού προσφέρουν ευκαιρίες για αποδοτική κρυπτογραφική επεξεργασία. Στο πλαίσιο αυτό, η παρούσα εργασία επικεντρώνεται στον σχεδιασμό και την υλοποίηση ενός ελαφροβαρούς κρυπτογραφικού συστήματος βασισμένου στον συμμετρικό κρυπτογραφικό αλγόριθμο Saturnin, σε συστοιχία επιτόπια προγραμματιζόμενων πυλών (Field Programmable Gate Array, FPGA). Η κρυπτογράφηση μπλοκ του Saturnin αποτελεί τη βάση του συστήματος κρυπτογράφησης με αυθεντικοποίηση (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data, AEAD) Saturnin -CTRCascade. Το σύστημα αυτό συνδυάζει την κρυπτογράφηση δεδομένων με τον έλεγχο αυθεντικότητας, επιτρέποντας την προστασία της εμπιστευτικότητας των μηνυμάτων και την ανίχνευση μη εξουσιοδοτημένων τροποποιήσεων. Το σύστημα που υλοποιήθηκε στην παρούσα εργασία υποστηρίζει την κρυπτογράφηση και την αποκρυπτογράφηση, καθώς και τη δημιουργία και την επαλήθευση των ετικετών αυθεντικοποίησης. Ο κύριος στόχος της εργασίας είναι η μετατροπή του αλγορίθμου σε μια αρχιτεκτονική υλικού που συνδυάζει τη σωστή λειτουργία με την αποδοτική χρήση των πόρων ενός συστήματος, δίνοντας ιδιαίτερη έμφαση στην οργάνωση των κρυπτογραφικών μετασχηματισμών, στον συντονισμό της κρυπτογράφησης και της πιστοποίησης, καθώς και στην επαναχρησιμοποίηση κοινών μονάδων επεξεργασίας. Η εργασία περιλαμβάνει τη μελέτη του αλγορίθμου, το σχεδιασμό των επιμέρους δομικών στοιχείων και την ενσωμάτωσή τους σε ένα ολοκληρωμένο κρυπτογραφικό σύστημα. Η λειτουργική επαλήθευση πραγματοποιείται τόσο σε επίπεδο των επιμέρους στοιχείων όσο και σε επίπεδο συστήματος μέσω σύγκρισης με ένα μοντέλο αναφοράς. Στη συνέχεια, η υλοποίηση αξιολογείται ως προς την απόδοσή της προκειμένου να εξεταστούν οι επιπτώσεις των αρχιτεκτονικών επιλογών και να εντοπιστούν ευκαιρίες για περαιτέρω ανάπτυξη.

title: Auditor OS / V50-S Sentinel Core: Reference Implementation
abstract: Auditor OS / V50-S Sentinel Core (Release v1.0.0) Production reference implementation of the Dual-Head Sentinel Core and the .sent Cryptographic Evidence Specification. Key Modules & Capabilities Stage I Prefill Audit (PrefillSentinelAuditor): Parallel prompt sequence evaluation, inter-layer contraction discordance checks, and agency-preserving context centroid extraction. Stage II Decode Governor (HardenedHomeostaticSentinelCore): Closed-loop thermodynamic regulation across the Informational Metric Interval ($\Delta\tau_t$), orthogonal shear decomposition ($a_\perp$), and $O(K \cdot d_{\text{model}})$ Fused Top-$K$ directional logit steering. Evidence Attestation (.sent Schema v1.0): Four-block canonical state hashing with Ed25519 signature binding and ephemeral session key infrastructure. Observer Isolation: Architectural specifications for AWS Nitro / AMD SEV-SNP confidential enclaves (docs/TEE_ENCLAVE_SPEC.md). Related Publications RFC-001 (.sent Specification): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23314793 AI Safety Paper: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23315812

title: Quantum-Secure Financial Settlement Systems: Zero-Knowledge Validation and Post-Quantum Ledger Interlocks
abstract: Global wholesale financial settlements, central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), and interbank clearing systems (e.g., SWIFT, Fedwire, TARGET2) rely almost exclusively on classical public-key cryptography—predominantly RSA-2048 and ECDSA. The advent of fault-tolerant quantum computing running Shor's factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms introduces an existential vulnerability: hostile actors harvesting encrypted ledger traffic under "Store Now, Decrypt Later" (SNDL) doctrines can retroactively forge historical balance proofs, forge settlement authorizations, and drain national foreign exchange reserves. Furthermore, existing post-quantum algorithmic patches (such as pure software PQC) do not protect against internal ledger manipulation, transaction censorship, or side-channel key extraction. This monograph establishes the formal mathematical architecture and hardware implementation blueprint for a **Quantum-Secure Financial Settlement System (QFS)** designed to defend sovereign economic fabrics against systemic post-quantum shocks: (1) We integrate high-speed Physical Quantum Random Number Generators (QRNGs) based on vacuum-state quantum fluctuations with balanced homodyne detection, injecting certified, irreproducible entropy at rates exceeding 10 Gbps; (2) We construct a Post-Quantum Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machine (**zkVM**) utilizing recursive STARK proofs over the 64-bit Goldilocks field (F_p, p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1), validating transaction validity, solvency, and compliance in zero-knowledge without leaking settlement counterparties, transaction amounts, or corporate account structures; (3) We formulate a dual-layer consensus interlock combining lattice-based digital signatures (ML-DSA-87 and Falcon-1024) with hardware-level PHOENIX_ROUTER physical interconnects, ensuring that cross-border clearing messages cannot be intercepted or modified; and (4) We establish autonomous circuit breakers enforcing sub-microsecond settlement freezes upon detecting non-quantum entropy anomalies. We demonstrate that this architecture satisfies regulatory capital standards under the Basel III/IV accords while fulfilling board fiduciary oversight duties under Delaware General Corporation Law.

title: Supplementary material: Post-Quantum Key Establishment over MAVLink: Measured Cost and Integration Pitfalls of HQC on a Small UAV
abstract: Supplementary material of the manuscript "Post-Quantum Key Establishment over MAVLink: Measured Cost and Integration Pitfalls of HQC on a Small UAV", submitted to IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems (resubmission of TAES-2026-2045). It contains the scripts that recompute every capture-derived result of Sections VI and VII of the manuscript (Tables V and VI, Fig. 3) from the public packet captures, the standalone test programs and recorded outputs of the KEM tests (known-answer test, self-consistency and benchmarks on a PC, a Raspberry Pi Pico and an ESP32), the patch that implements the corrections for findings F2 to F6 together with the activation self-test, the MAVLink dialect message list, and the handshake transcript and key schedule as the flight-controller firmware computes them. The evaluated firmware and the packet captures are not included: they are the ArduPilot fork at commit b402392 of cdcp2/ardupilot_post_quantum_kem (cloned with --recursive), which the manuscript cites. The ground-station software was not archived.

title: Machine learning-based pathomics signature as a novel digital marker for C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 9 expression and prognostic assessment in breast cancer
abstract: Objectives: C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 9 (CXCL9) is a critical mediator of tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte recruitment and a potential biomarker in breast cancer (BC). This study aimed to develop a machine learning-based handcrafted pathomics model to forecast survival outcomes by characterizing CXCL9-related morphological signatures from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides. The biological relevance and clinical utility of the derived pathomics score (PS) were subsequently evaluated to provide an objective framework for risk stratification. Material and Methods: We developed a pathomics model integrating quantitative H&E image features with machine learning in 791 Cancer Genome Atlas-BC patients. Feature selection using minimum redundancy maximum relevance and recursive feature elimination was performed exclusively within the training set, and a gradient boosting machine model was constructed to output a PS representing the predicted probability of CXCL9 expression. Model performance was assessed in the training, testing, and external validation cohorts. Associations of PS with survival, immune infiltration, cancer-immunity cycle (CI cycle) activity, tumor mutational burden, and molecular subtypes were investigated through integrated bioinformatics. Results: CXCL9 expression was confirmed as a significant prognostic factor for overall survival ( P = 0.037). The pathomics model demonstrated stable performance for predicting CXCL9 status in training, testing, and external cohorts (area under the curves: 0.741, 0.729, and 0.704, respectively). The PS significantly correlated with CXCL9 expression, stratified patients into distinct prognostic groups ( P = 0.012), and remained a significant protective factor in multivariate analysis (hazard ratio = 0.66, P = 0.048). Mechanistically, high PS was associated with immune-inflamed features, characterized by increased natural killer cells and CD8+ T-cell infiltration, enhanced CI cycle activity, and elevated TMB. Furthermore, the PS effectively reflected clinical heterogeneity, with triple-negative BC exhibiting the highest scores compared to other molecular subtypes ( P <0.001). Conclusion: This pathomics framework provides an imaging-derived indicator of CXCL9 expression and may support prognostic stratification in BC. Its association with immune-inflamed characteristics suggests potential relevance for immune phenotype assessment, but its value for predicting immunotherapy response requires validation in immunotherapy-treated cohorts.

title: SENTIMENT ANALYSIS BASED ON THE PERFORMANCE ASPECTS OF THE TIKTOK APP BY TIME PERIOD AND APP VERSION USING SUPPORT VECTOR MACHINES (SVM)
abstract: This study aims to analyze aspect-based sentiment regarding the performance of the TikTok app based on user reviews on Google Play, as well as to identify changes in user perceptions over time and across app versions following app updates. The performance aspects analyzed include speed, stability, and responsiveness. This study employs a quantitative method with a descriptive approach. Data was obtained through web scraping of TikTok user reviews on Google Play during the period of January 1–December 31, 2025. The data was processed through the stages of text preprocessing, sentiment labeling using the INSET lexicon, aspect labeling using a keyword-based approach, feature representation using TF-IDF, and classification using the Support Vector Machine (SVM) method. The results of the study indicate that SVM is capable of effectively classifying sentiment across all aspects of the app’s performance. Speed and stability were the most frequently discussed aspects and were dominated by negative sentiment. Additionally, the analysis revealed that app updates influenced changes in user perceptions of TikTok’s performance throughout 2025.Keywords: aspect-based sentiment analysis, TikTok, SVM.

title: Supporting Private and Efficient Consumer Requests to Data Brokers
abstract: Under data privacy regulations, such as GDPR and CCPA, consumers are legally entitled to access, delete, or opt-out from collection of, personal information that so-called data brokers collect about them. However, the process of exercising these rights remains non-uniform, inefficient, and privacy-invasive. A consumer must submit individual requests to hundreds of data brokers, each requiring different - and often extensive - identity verification procedures. In January 2026, California launched a centralized facility that allows consumers to formulate a single (unified) request to all registered data brokers. While this simplifies the process, it raises significant privacy, scalability, and security concerns. Current commercial services (e.g., DeleteMe and Incogni) automate such requests for a fee, although they require consumers to provide all personal information upfront to yet another entity of uncertain trustworthiness.
