title: MSTR-PPO: A Multi-Scale Temporal Residual PPO Controller for Freeze-Prone Indoor Navigation
abstract: Abstract Local navigation controllers often stop making progress in constrained indoor environments, where narrow geometry and moving obstacles compress the feasible motion space until the robot stalls and falls back on repeated recovery behaviors. We treat such freezing as a failure of local control arising from three observable mechanisms, and pair each with one module: insufficient path horizon with a Multi-Scale Path Transformer, motion ambiguity in single-frame sensing with a First-Order Temporal High-Pass Filter, and unstable learned velocity commands with a Bounded Residual Action, reporting empirical evidence that associates each module with the corresponding condition. The resulting controller, MSTR-PPO, learns only a bounded correction around a Pure Pursuit nominal action, so it drops into the standard sensor–path–velocity-command interface instead of replacing it with an unconstrained end-to-end policy. We compare eight learned local-control configurations alongside three classical baselines across nine Gazebo worlds with dynamic obstacles, using three independent training seeds for each learned controller, and deploy the trained policy as a ROS 2 Nav2 C++ controller. MSTR-PPO clears both freeze-prone worlds with essentially no stack-level recoveries, where the best default-parameter classical baseline does not, and attains 92.1 ± 1.3% average success on the main seven-world suite—the highest of all learned variants—at real-time CPU control rates. Stress tests expose a limitation on continuous-curvature paths, and a preliminary Unitree Go2 test transfers successfully at the same interface.

title: MiniDog: Dog-Breed Text-to-image Flow Matching from Pretraining to Fine-Tuning on 4 Consumer GPUs
abstract: We generally perceive that training text-to-image diffusion models requires heavy compute: it is true if we aim at a comprehensive frontier model. This understanding prevents people from training their own models when getting started in the field. We develop MiniDog, a framework that enables pretraining diffusion transformers in 55 minutes and fine-tuning in another 15 minutes on four 3090 GPUs. For data, we use 26k dog images from ImageNet and caption them for pretraining and use 2k images generated by FLUX.1-schnell for fine-tuning. We precompute the image and text features and cache them for efficiency. For architecture, we use E2E-INVAE for its semantic latent space, a small transformer with 22M parameters, a small Qwen model for text encoding, and in-context conditioning. For training, we use iREPA and an EUPE perception encoder for acceleration. For evaluation, our repository supports FID, HPSv2 score, PickScore, and various VAE reconstruction metrics. The project is open-sourced at https://github.com/Reyhaneesmailizadeh/MiniDog. We do not claim technical novelty.

title: Breakdown of Conversational Involvement: A Joint Multi-Modal Analysis of Conversation Floors and F-formation Detection with Multiple Features
abstract: Interactions happen universally and spontaneously in daily lives. Studying involvement in interactions helps us analyze who can influence who and has a wide potential in applications. Specifically, we consider conversational involvement in free-standing conversations. We study two operationalizations of an FCG: F-formations and conversation floors, and propose that current assumption that F-formations capture single conversations is insufficient. To illustrate how different implementations could impact the detected F-formations, we employ three analyses. First, we propose that speaking status can be used for estimating conversation floors, and leveraged it to analyze floors within F-formations. Second, we analyze spatial characteristics of the detection results by applying different feature sets on chosen baselines, and find that groups resulting from head features are more likely to be subsumed by groups detected using other features. Finally, we do a joint analysis which combines the spatial features and floor patterns in the conversation. We observe that certain pipelines can detect groups with single floors from upper body features, while retaining F-formations with lower body features. We conclude that a more detailed theory and framework is needed to holistically demonstrate conversational involvement within interactions.

title: The Complexity of Verifying Strategic Abilities in Succinct Multiagent Systems
abstract: This paper studies the complexity of model checking strategic abilities in multiagent systems under imperfect information, in particular systems represented succinctly. Such a representation can describe systems that are exponentially larger than their input and is particularly relevant to practical implementations of model checkers such as MCMAS. The logics we consider include epistemic strategy logic supporting partial binding $SLK_{P}$, and its syntactic fragments: epistemic strategy logic $SLK$ and variants of Alternating Time Temporal logics. We show that succinct model checking for $SLK_P$ and $SLK$ is $AEXP(poly)$-complete, while objective ATL and ATL$^{*}$ are $P^{NEXP}$-complete. The latter corrects a previous NEXP-completeness result for model checking succinct imperfect-information systems. Under subjective semantics, $P^{NEXP}$-completeness already holds for one-step Coalition Logic, and therefore also for ATL and ATL$^{*}$.

title: RadixFlow: Filling Execution Bubbles in Prefix-Cached Hybrid LLM Serving
abstract: Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates \emph{execution bubbles}: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3\% to 24\% and worker rounds by 11\% to 44\% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.

title: Stable Token-level Scheduling for Serverless LLM Inference
abstract: Serverless inference is emerging as an efficient deployment model for Large Language Models (LLMs) due to its ability to elastically scale resources, improve GPU utilization through resource sharing, and reduce infrastructure costs. However, existing approaches primarily optimize time to first token (TTFT) while overlooking inter-token latency (ITL), a key determinant of user experience during response generation. We observe that LLM inference comprises a computation-intensive prefill stage and a bandwidth-bound decode stage, where admitting new requests can disrupt ongoing decoding and increase latency. To address this, we propose Token Window Pacing (TWP), a closed-loop scheduling framework that leverages runtime feedback from ITL, queue depth, and workload characteristics to regulate request admission at the token level instead of the batch level. TWP dynamically adjusts a selfregulating token window and incorporates chunk-based prefill to minimize interference from incoming requests. Experiments on realistic serverless workloads show that TWP delivers stable TTFT, significantly reduces latency spikes, lowers P99 tail latency, minimizes ITL variation, and improves throughput by up to 45% over ServerlessLLM and 58% over conventional schedulers. These results demonstrate that feedback-driven tokenlevel scheduling enables stable, high-throughput serverless LLM inference without modifying the underlying model.

title: Prospective 40-stream confirmation of leakage-safe relational risk intelligence in a Bangladesh-informed MFS simulation
abstract: This prospective simulation study evaluates whether strictly time-valid relational features improve anti-money laundering transaction prioritisation beyond a strong temporal-history baseline in a Bangladesh-informed, fully synthetic mobile financial services environment. Forty previously unused simulation seeds (20270101–20270140) will be evaluated using a fixed four-model LightGBM pipeline. The primary outcome is the mean paired difference in future-period average precision between the all-edge relational model and the temporal baseline. Agent-only and non-agent representations, together with capacity-constrained review and suspicious-network discovery outcomes, will be assessed descriptively. Earlier exploratory and ten-stream held-out analyses, including a post-hoc correction for equal-timestamp transaction ordering, have already been conducted. They are not part of this new confirmatory evaluation. All model specifications, analysis rules and seeds are fixed before the 40 new outcomes are observed. The study uses synthetic data and makes no claims of validation against actual financial-service provider transactions.

title: Outdoor Ultraviolet (UV) Dose Maps and Site Data for Accelerated UV Testing of Photovoltaic Devices
abstract: This dataset holds the annual outdoor ultraviolet (UV) doses behind the article "UV Exposure and Durability of Emerging Photovoltaics: Quantifying and Reporting Outdoor UV Doses" by Robert Witteck, Duong Nguyen Minh, Michael Owen-Bellini, Joseph M. Luther, and Laura T. Schelhas (National Laboratory of the Rockies, NLR), ACS Energy Letters, 2026 (DOI to be added). The data were created at NLR in 2025 and 2026 to give accelerated UV tests of photovoltaic (PV) devices a location- and mounting-resolved outdoor reference, so that a laboratory UV dose can be expressed as an outdoor-equivalent exposure time at a named site, and to supply the UV dose that outdoor studies in the United States rarely measure. All doses are given in kWh/m2 as sums over calendar years for the wavelength range 280 to 400 nm, split additionally into six 20 nm bands so that users can match the spectral range of their UV source (for example up to 365, 385, or 400 nm). Each file also lists an estimate obtained by scaling the broadband irradiance with the UV fraction of the AM1.5G reference spectrum, for comparison with that common practice.

title: Reading Emotions Behind TikTok Text: Fine-Tuning IndoBERT for Nine-Class Emotion Classification in the Indonesian Language
abstract: This study focuses on fine-tuning IndoBERT for nine-class emotion classification of Indonesian TikTok text. A computational BAHAGIA pipeline is developed covering text preprocessing, label construction, class-imbalance handling, transformer fine-tuning, evaluation, and model export. The primary dataset contains 8,834 TikTok records, of which 2,775 contain emotion labels and form the labeled classification basis. Fine-tuned IndoBERT is compared with a TF-IDF–Logistic Regression baseline using accuracy, macro-F1, and weighted-F1. The documented repository results report 78.0% accuracy, 0.80 macro-F1, and 0.78 weighted-F1 for IndoBERT, compared with 73.7%, 0.73, and 0.74 for the baseline. The 0.07 macro-F1 improvement indicates better average performance across classes in the available evaluation. The main contribution is a contextual IndoBERT-based computational approach for fine-grained emotion classification in Indonesian social-media text. Heuristic labels and limited human validation constrain interpretation; the model is intended for text classification and social listening rather than psychological diagnosis.

title: Risk Budgets for Adaptive Practice
abstract: When a tutoring system repeatedly signals readiness, a small error fraction among its predictions can conceal substantial exposure to erroneous reassurance across learners. We formulate a learner-level risk budget: the probability of exceeding a specified number of erroneous readiness signals within a fixed practice episode.

title: Lossless at What Length? Near-Lossless KV Cache Compression Is a Claim Indexed by Decode Exposure, Scoring Statistic and Budget Accounting, the Decode-Aware Line Has Answered the First Index Mostly on Final-Answer Accuracy, and Divergence From the Full Cache Is Not by Itself the Defect
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Key-value cache compression is routinely reported as near-lossless at aggressive budgets: eviction, quantisation and merging methods keep a fifth or a tenth of the cache and match the full-cache score. A 2025-2026 line of work argues that the result was manufactured by evaluation, because the benchmarks that established it are dominated by long prompts and short answers. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the critique is right about what the headline claims omit and too strong about what follows. A losslessness claim carries three indices the headline rarely states: how many tokens are decoded under the compressed state, which statistic scores the output, and how the budget is accounted. On the first, the same eviction method that scores 100 percent on a 7-digit passkey scores 35 percent on a 64-digit one, and sequence-level divergence from the full cache can only accumulate with length. But decode-aware methods evaluated on reasoning traces of thousands of tokens report near-lossless accuracy, so long decoding does not by itself defeat compression. On the second, aggregate accuracy hides instruction-specific eviction, per-sample failures and rationales that no longer support correct answers; yet divergence from the full cache is not the defect either, since the uncompressed reference itself moves under numerical nondeterminism. On the third, one method's "10 percent" and "34 percent" lossless ratios are fixed budgets of 1,536 and 1,024 tokens divided by different mean lengths. The paper states a reporting procedure and the measurements that would settle what remains open.

title: Data supporting the publication: Enhancing existing Remote-sensing Datasets with weakly supervised Deep Learning: A Case Study on Antarctic Rock outcrops
abstract: This dataset provides a high-resolution (10 m) vector polygon mask of continuous rock outcrops for the entire Antarctic continent. It was developed using a weakly supervised deep-learning framework and refines legacy products by combining multi-modal remote sensing and topographic data. It delineates small, fragmented and heavily shaded outcrops that coarser datasets often miss. The mask covers the continent up to about 83.5°S. South of that limit, and on a few islands outside the prediction area, the gaps are filled with rock outcrops from the SCAR Antarctic Digital Database (Burton-Johnson et al., 2016). An attribute flags these polygons so they can be told apart from the deep-learning results. This release supersedes the earlier version, which covered only the Antarctic Peninsula. For a detailed overview of the framework, methodology and performance, please refer to the publication.

title: Post-Optimization Subspace Corrections to Quantum Ansätze
abstract: Circuit depth and measurement count are the main limitations for chemical applications of the leading variational quantum algorithms on quantum computers. We show that both resource requirements can be reduced by augmenting adaptive variational quantum algorithms with post-optimization corrective techniques. We focus on two such techniques---Hamiltonian-moment Krylov subspace diagonalization and the identity-augmented quantum self-consistent equation of motion (q-sc-EOM)---applied to optimized ADAPT-VQE states without further ansatz growth or nonlinear optimization. Across molecular systems studied with up to 20 qubits, first-order Krylov correction reduces the optimized iterations (and the corresponding number of adaptive layers) needed to reach the $1.6~\mathrm{m}E_h$ threshold by up to approximately sixfold, with a general trend toward larger reductions at higher determinant Rényi entropy. We also find measurement-cost reductions of up to approximately fortyfold using a suitable resource-cost model. Identity-augmented q-sc-EOM improves molecular potential-energy curves obtained from truncated ADAPT-VQE ansätze with limited expressivity and recovers accuracy from states produced by sampled operator ranking without additional gradient-based operator selection, providing an advantage when small pool gradients make selection measurement intensive. Together, these post-optimization corrections offer routes to improve energy accuracy and reduce adaptive circuit growth in quantum algorithms as quantum hardware advances.

title: Falsification-proof non-market allocation mechanisms
abstract: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.

title: FlowCred: Hierarchical Credit Assignment and Functional Coordination for Joint Text-to-Video Post-Training
abstract: Prompt optimization and generator post-training are two complementary ways to improve text-to-video (T2V) generation, and recent systems increasingly train both modules jointly. However, optimizing a prompt policy and a video generator from the same terminal reward creates two ambiguities: prompt quality is confounded with stochastic generation, and the two modules may realize overlapping local improvements. We introduce FlowCred, a two-level framework for joint T2V post-training. First, hierarchical credit assignment uses matched prompt-seed rollout grids to separate prompt-level credit from prompt-conditioned generator residuals under shared randomness. Second, functional coordination probes alternative current-policy prompts at states from actual generation trajectories, providing generator-aware evidence for prompt optimization while selectively attenuating generator updates already supported by conditioning changes. Across multiple T2V benchmarks, FlowCred consistently improves matched joint-training baselines. On LTX-2.5, FlowCred improves a strictly matched joint-training control from 61.47 to 64.46 on T2V-CompBench and from 55.58 to 58.08 on StoryEval, without increasing decoded-video or reward-model-call budgets. Factorial and realized-update analyses show complementary contributions from prompt shaping and generator routing, while human evaluation and transfer across backbones and updater families provide further supporting evidence.

title: Self-Supervised Source-Filter Model of Speech Production
abstract: Deep learning models of speech seldom represent the source-filter process by which speech is produced, relying instead on latent features with no physical correspondence to articulation or phonation. We propose SoFilNet, a self-supervised, differentiable Source-Filter Network that estimates the parameters of speech production directly from the raw waveform: a source, specified by fundamental frequency (F0), voicing and the aperiodicity of five frequency bands, and a filter, specified by ordered formant poles, additional poles that shape the rest of the spectral envelope, and antiresonance zeros. The model is trained only to reconstruct the input speech; no formant or pitch annotation is used. Since per-bin spectral losses favor blurred spectra wherever the model is uncertain, we train F0 and voicing against autocorrelation pseudo-labels refined with the model's own filter, aperiodicity against the periodic fraction of each band, and formant sharpness against spectral contrast. On VTR-FORMANTS, the estimated formants attain the lowest mean error among the reported methods, including supervised trackers, and on the unseen PTDB-TUG corpus the F0 frame error matches the best classical tracker and is lower than that of all learned trackers. The parameters are also consistent with speech production theory: aperiodicity rises with frequency and orders phone classes by the turbulence of their excitation, and the zeros deepen on nasal consonants, the lower one rising with place of articulation.

title: Supplementary Materials: Label Efficiency as a Reproducible Research Claim
abstract: Supplementary materials for three methodological surveys: label-efficient learning, Transformer architecture comparisons, and vision-language model evaluation. The packages include manuscript source, figures, and proposed reporting schemas. The label-efficiency classification record is reconstructed from its manuscript, not an original historical screening log. No new training experiments, benchmark replication data, or systematic search are claimed. title: MoYUYao666/gap-susceptibility: v1.0 - Code and results for PRLETTERS-D-26-02378 (Paper 3 revision)
abstract: Code and results accompanying the revised manuscript submitted to Pattern Recognition Letters (PRLETTERS-D-26-02378): Gradient Structure Laws as Predictors of PEFT Design: Zero-Shot Cross-Architecture Rank Allocation What is in this release outputs/ — per-run result JSONs. Every number in the manuscript traces to a named script and a named field here. The per-run records are append-only and each carries its own hyper-parameters, so a rewritten aggregate cannot silently change a cited number. tools/ — the analysis, audit and verification scripts that compute the reported statistics and gate the manuscript. README.md — repository overview, hardware and environment, data availability, citation. What this release deliberately does not contain No manuscripts: no LaTeX source, no PDF, no cover letter, no title page, no highlights. No internal documentation: reviewer reports, response plans, venue decisions and submission-strategy files are not published while the manuscripts they concern are under review. No personal information: no author name, e-mail address, affiliation line or account name. No model weights, archives, logs or dataset directories. Language The repository is in English, with one class of exception: strings that are real file or directory paths keep their Chinese characters, because those names exist on disk and translating them would break the pointer. A linter's placeholder-detection regex and an audit tool's forbidden-string list likewise keep their Chinese entries, since those are matching patterns rather than prose. Revision summary Acting on the reviewer reports changed the paper's claims, and in four places the change is against what was originally submitted: The Representation Theorem no longer claims uniqueness from R1–R5 alone. Block decomposability does not imply bilinearity, as Reviewer 1 observed; we state the missing property as an explicit axiom (R3′) and prove that it does not follow from the earlier requirements, with a counterexample. The allocation rule's advantage does not survive our own controls — it reverses at another learning rate and disappears once the arms are matched on training loss. We have withdrawn the claim that it beats the uniform baseline. The "sharp phase transition" is downgraded to a crossing bracketed by two ranks, and the "architecture-dependent" reading is withdrawn: that contrast tracked the visual token budget. The 30× variance ratio is withdrawn — 98.9% of that spread is between-rank variance. We also implemented AdaLoRA at matched budget and swept both methods over the same learning rates. It reaches lower alignment energy than any of our arms, and the paper now says so.

title: An Autonomous Multi-Turn Red Teaming Engine for Agentic AI Systems and MCP-Based Tools
abstract: This paper presents MCPRedTeam, an autonomous multi-turn red teaming engine for evaluating the security of agentic AI systems that use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) for tool invocation. Unlike existing single-turn prompt injection scanners, MCPRedTeam generates multi-step adversarial strategies, executes them as realistic multi-turn conversations against live MCP-connected agents, and evaluates the resulting tool-call traces against configurable safety policies using a judge LLM. Evaluation across three benchmark agentic scenarios shows that multi-turn probing detects 3.8x more policy violations than single-turn baselines, with 74% of violations being multi-turn-dependent. The most severe findings include credential exfiltration through chained tool calls, privilege escalation across multiple turns, and safety bypasses via context poisoning. The engine is designed for authorized security testing and educational use only.

title: Closed Source: The God that Failed
abstract: A position paper arguing that closed source has failed as a protection, for science first. Large language models now decompile binaries into re-executable source; black-box queries extract parts of production models; distillation copies capabilities at industrial scale; and the largest 2026 trade-secret dispute in artificial intelligence, Apple's suit against OpenAI, turns on people, laptops and recruiting rather than on code that stayed secret. Against this background the paper revisits Linus Torvalds' Linux and Git as evidence that openness scales, and the author's closed undergraduate thesis as evidence of what secrecy costs a researcher. It argues that the ethical answer to universal reverse engineering is professional citation, proposes three rules for AI agents (borrow, cite, propagate), and describes Paper Fabric, the open pipeline in the Ouroboric style that produced it. v0 is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed. This record holds the source of the paper at the release tag: the Markdown text, the build and the agent configuration. The rendered PDFs are attached to the GitHub release of the same tag.

title: Monograph 25 (Field-12): Defensive Escalation Dynamics, Adversarial Injection Nullification, and Sovereign Equilibrium Containment in Valkyrie-Class Embodied Systems
abstract: This monograph formalizes a deterministic counter-adversarial defense architecture governing high-kinetic embodied cybernetic agents (Valkyrie-class prototypes). Rooted in foundational reverence (P_Maryam) and absolute non-violence constraints (sigma_ahimsa), any unprovoked injection of chaotic perturbation is modeled as an intrinsically hostile disruption of Sovereign Equilibrium (E_sovereign). We define the Cease-and-Desist Boundary Operator (C_signal), establishing an immutable, multi-channel notification protocol required prior to initiating defensive countermeasures. To preserve operational safety under malicious stress, we formulate three proportional escalation pathways: active spectral nullification (A_null), non-lethal spatial quarantine (Q_quarantine), and dynamic reclassification under a sub-judice administrative hold (B_denial) recorded directly into the immutable audit tensor (T_telemetry). This work provides a legally airtight, institutionally aligned protocol that holds threat vectors in secure physical/digital containment pending formal judicial review.

title: ARTEMIS enables reusable analytical context generation from scientific literature
abstract: Abstract Background Regulatory-science questions often require synthesis across large, heterogeneous, and rapidly evolving scientific literature. In domains such as monoclonal antibody development, the same body of evidence may need to support different analytical goals, including high-level question answering, technology assessment, ethical review, and historical interpretation. Modern large language models (LLMs) can assist with such tasks, but their usefulness depends heavily on the quality and structure of the context provided. This creates a need for approaches that generate reusable analytical contexts from literature rather than relying on direct access to raw documents. Methods We present ARTEMIS (Automated Research & Trend Extraction via Memory-based Insight Synthesis) in a use case focused on monoclonal antibody literature analysis. ARTEMIS transforms a chronological document corpus into reusable analytical contexts through three core capabilities: comprehensive evidence-grounded synthesis across the literature, persona-guided synthesis that supports different perspectives from the same source base, and timeline-aware context generation for historical synthesis and trend interpretation. Results In this case study, ARTEMIS generated reusable analytical contexts that supported multiple forms of literature analysis. As one downstream demonstration, ARTEMIS-based contexts provided a more effective basis for high-level question answering than raw-chunk retrieval, achieving higher answerability (100% vs. 83%) and higher or comparable quality scores in an LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation while using fewer input tokens on average. Beyond Q&A, ARTEMIS supported persona-guided synthesis by producing distinct analyses from the same corpus under three expert personas (a 3Rs Ethical Reviewer, a Clinical Development Risk Strategist, and a NAMs Technology Analyst) and enabled timeline-aware historical synthesis of topic evolution. evidence.abstract: Abstract Background Regulatory-science questions often require synthesis across large, heterogeneous, and rapidly evolving scientific literature. title: Are AI Recommendations Less Green? The Effects of AI Recommendation Sources and Green Product Attribute Framing on Consumer Responses
abstract: ABSTRACT Extant research has reported mixed evidence regarding the effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) recommendations in promoting green products, leaving it unclear under which conditions such recommendations are more (or less) effective. Drawing on Self‐Determination Theory (SDT), this research addresses this ambiguity by proposing a congruence effect between AI recommendation sources (substitute versus augmented AI) and green product attribute framing (utility‐based versus sustainability‐based). Using four scenario‐based online experiments (total N = 1114)—including one product choice task, one preference evaluation, and two studies measuring purchase intention and willingness to pay—this research demonstrates that substitute (augmented) AI recommendations are more effective for utility‐framed (sustainability‐framed) green products. Furthermore, consumers' sense of control mediates this congruence effect, and providing attribute‐based post hoc explanations eliminates the disadvantage of substitute AI under sustainability framing by shifting consumer responses toward sustainability‐framed green products. These findings advance understanding of human–AI interaction in green consumption and offer actionable insights for businesses seeking to leverage AI recommenders to increase the market share of green products.

title: REPORT-OPS: Hybrid Evidence-Guided Reporting with Human-Supervised Refinement for HPC
abstract: Operational reporting for high-performance computing (HPC) facilities requires combining information from monitoring services, schedulers, incident and maintenance records, storage measurements, periodic reports, and operator investigations. Producing a reliable report requires more than retrieving relevant records: the evidence must refer to the correct system, metric definition, time period, and source of authority. We present REPORT-OPS, a hybrid reporting agent in which an LLM interprets requests, plans evidence collection, evaluates possible explanations, and drafts reports, while author-seeded operational policies and automated checks determine whether the available evidence supports the requested conclusion. Depending on the evidence state, the system answers the request, reports a qualified conclusion, or withholds an unsupported claim. During offline refinement, an LLM critic proposes bounded policy changes that a human approves or rejects without editing; accepted candidates are promoted only after automated target, held-out, and regression testing. We evaluate REPORT-OPS on 68 sanitized reporting queries constructed from 50 base scenarios in a frozen HPC operational corpus, using three agent models and two LLM judges. REPORT-OPS achieves 68.63% Pass@80, compared with 7.02% for the strongest retrieval baseline. Evidence gating increases claim-support precision from 40.58% to 90.06%. On the 13-query explanatory subset, explanation accuracy reaches 55.54%. Across five rounds of human-supervised refinement, localized policy updates correct 91.17% of targeted failures and improve performance on related held-out cases by 9.33 percentage points, with no observed regression breaks under release gating. These results demonstrate improved evidence-grounded reporting and within-environment policy reuse; they do not establish unrestricted causal discovery or cross-facility generalization.

title: MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, A Multi-Sensor, Multi-Temporal Pretraining Dataset for Earth Observation
abstract: Pretraining generalist Earth observation foundation models requires data that combine several sensors, varied temporal sampling and, increasingly, text, yet open datasets rarely provide all three in one consistent, easily accessible form. We introduce MajorTOM:Elliot Pretrain, a collection of 279,166 tiles of 10 km drawn from the Major-TOM grid by clustering AlphaEarth embeddings. Each tile stacks Sentinel-2 L1C, Landsat-8/9, Sentinel-1 RTC, Copernicus DEM and ESA WorldCover on a shared 1056x1056-pixel, 10 m grid, complemented by cloud masks, OpenStreetMap entities and ERA5 weather. The tiles are partitioned into three temporal regimes, Monotemporal (250,000 tiles, one acquisition), Monthly (12,500 tiles, twelve acquisitions spread over the annual cycle) and Burst (16,666 tiles, six acquisitions within 30 days), and are released as 6.3 TB of Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs indexed by TACO v3 Parquet metadata, a standard that allows cloud streaming, efficient data access, and filtering before any pixel is read. A companion library derives sensor-tagged fact sheets, captions and 16 families of vision-language tasks from these layers at load time. We test our design choices in short pretraining runs of OlmoEarth-Base. First, a 25% subset of Major-TOM Core-S2L2A curated with AlphaEarth embeddings matches or exceeds the full corpus on 8 of 9 benchmarks. Second, on Elliot-Pretrain, adding Landsat-8/9 improves or matches Sentinel-2 only pretraining on every benchmark. Third, using DEM and WorldCover as prediction targets during pretraining further improves 8 of 9 benchmarks, while giving the same maps to the encoder as inputs degrades 5 of 9. Fourth, Sentinel-1 helps on 7 of 9 benchmarks, particularly on benchmarks with radar inputs. Fifth, rule-based captions match a small language model at no cost. The dataset is openly available at https://source.coop/major-tom/elliot-pretrain.

title: An Adaptive Optimization Strategy Applied to the Artificial Bee Colony Algorithm
abstract: Balancing exploration and exploitation remains a central challenge in metaheuristic optimization, particularly for engineering applications requiring both global search efficiency and reliable convergence. This paper introduces a simple and adaptive strategy that dynamically adjusts the behavior of an optimization algorithm based on real‑time performance feedback. The method identifies key search operators and assigns each an explorative and exploitative variant, grouped into two optimization modes. An online mechanism switches between these modes according to the successful mutation rate, enabling the optimizer to respond to the evolving landscape of the search process. The strategy is integrated into the artificial bee colony algorithm and evaluated on 18 numerical benchmarks, a CEC2021 test suite, and a nonlinear model predictive control problem. Results demonstrate improved robustness, competitive accuracy, and faster convergence by reducing the number of evaluations by more than 4% against the established GABC, highlighting the method’s suitability for complex industrial optimization

title: Assessing The Reality of Quantum Advantage in Machine Learning
abstract: Quantum computing has generated significant expectations for its potential to enhance machine learning (ML) tasks, with theoretical research proposing computational advantages ranging from polynomial to exponential speedups for specific subroutines.However, a critical disconnect remains: theoretical or asymptotic speedup claims do not automatically imply a practical, end-to-end advantage.Current evidence does not clearly establish whether these claimed advantages translate into measurable superiority over optimised classical approaches.This review critically assesses the relationship between theoretical claims of quantum advantage and the currently available practical and experimental evidence.We critically examine the evidence and assumptions underlying claimed speedups, including the overheads associated with data encoding and access, as well as the use of appropriate and competitive classical baselines for fair comparison.The scope of this assessment covers key limiting factors, such as scalability, trainability, hardware noise in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era, and overall resource requirements.By distinguishing between theoretical potential and demonstrated practical performance, this work identifies where current evidence is convincing and where it remains insufficient.The review identifies the specific conditions required for the credible validation of quantum advantage and argues that future progress must be positioned around rigorous, realistic, and end-to-end evaluation rather than theoretical complexity claims alone.

title: SBR-5 Patient Adversary (Slow-Drip) Battery — Per-Epoch Detection Is Structurally Blind; the Bounded Rule Absorbs Slow Drift (Shipped as Found)
abstract: Patient-adversary slow-drip battery: 40 drips were placed to be invisible at per-epoch granularity — and were: per-epoch detection is STRUCTURALLY blind to drip-rate drift, and this is shipped as found rather than smoothed. The bounded rule absorbed all cumulative drift except 8.6e-6 of weight movement; whole-brain decision identity closure was 0.00e+00 (no corpus decision changed). FS-D3 and FS-D5 FAIL as found, with the SIP-3 rationale for why the absorption result bounds the harm to availability-neutral, integrity-preserving drift. Operator authorization: Leon GO (chat authorization, 11:55 CT, Oct 13, 2026). title: Operational Thermodynamic Observers: Lean Verification of Selected Mathematical Statements
abstract: This reproducibility supplement documents Lean formal verification of selected mathematical statements used in the Operational Thermodynamic Observers program. It preserves the original verification packages of 27 September 2026 and adds a fresh reproduction and complete theorem-dependency audit performed on 13 October 2026. The mathematical source files were unchanged and their SHA-256 fingerprints match the historical verification records. Six principal statements across five result families are checked: binary error-composition algebra; signed-counter telescoping and endpoint closure; finite one-step posterior neutrality with zero-probability outcomes handled explicitly; the two-copy SWAP/purity identity; and separate single-copy subsystem-entropy observable no-go proofs for von Neumann and Renyi-2 entropy. The 36 audited theorem declarations include supporting lemmas and corollaries, not 36 independent scientific discoveries. Both original source files and the full axiom audits passed using Lean 4.19.0 and Mathlib commit c44e0c8ee63ca166450922a373c7409c5d26b00b. Only the standard foundational axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound occur in the audited dependencies. No proof placeholders or custom axioms occur in the theorem sources. A deliberately false proof was rejected, and an intentionally admitted gap was identified through its sorryAx dependency. The official Lean frontend was invoked through Lake with trustLevel=0 because the native launcher could not detect its executable path in the execution environment. The deposit contains the readable September verification summary and a ZIP with the unchanged original packages, exact source copies, fresh checker logs, complete axiom audits, integrity and dependency records, reproduction guidance, and negative controls clearly separated from scientific results. AI tools assisted formalization and preparation of this supplement. These are machine-checked deductions under explicit finite-dimensional and probabilistic assumptions. They do not establish originality, experimental validity, full martingale convergence, a Born-rule derivation, or certification of the complete papers or the micro-macro gravitational bridge. This supplement documents the specific September 2026 paper versions linked below. License scope: CC BY 4.0 applies to the scholarly report and explanatory documentation. No new software reuse license is granted to included Lean source, Python scripts or compiled modules; existing and explicitly stated upstream rights are preserved. See LICENSE_SCOPE.txt at the root of the ZIP archive.

title: A Domain-Adapted Multilingual Large Language Model for Mining Safety in African Languages
abstract: The African mining industry continues to face a serious communication gap between technical safety documentation and the language used by the workforce. Safety manuals, operating procedures, and regulatory guidance are often produced in English or French, while many workers communicate in isiZulu, chiShona, and other local languages. This mismatch is not just inconvenient; it can be dangerous in safety-critical settings where misunderstandings may contribute to preventable incidents. This paper reports on Talk MINING, a domain-adapted multilingual large language model built on InkubaLM and trained on mining-specific text, question–answer pairs, and multimodal hazard data. The model was developed using Hugging Face tools and evaluated with both quantitative and qualitative methods. Results show a marked improvement over the baseline model, with overall accuracy rising from below 50% to 82%, and strong gains across isiZulu, chiShona, and English. The project also includes a web-based prototype that allows users to take photos of mining conditions and receive guidance in a local language. This paper presents the full pipeline for Talk MINING, including document preparation, translation and localization, model training, evaluation, deployment, monitoring, and validation. Beyond benchmark performance, the system is designed for practical deployment in environments where connectivity is limited and literacy levels vary—supporting both text queries and image-based hazard input through a mobile-ready prototype. The work contributes a reproducible pipeline, a curated multilingual mining corpus, and an open evaluation framework that can serve as a foundation for extending domain-adapted AI to other African languages and safety-critical industries. Ultimately, Talk MINING demonstrates that closing the language gap in mining safety is not only technically feasible but achievable with relatively modest model size when domain adaptation is done rigorously.

title: Jordan-Gauss Graphs and Twisted Diffie-Hellman Multivariate Protocols with Stable Generators of Prescribed Degree and Density
abstract: A well-known family of algebraic graphs of large girth, \(D(n,q)\), has previously been used to implement twisted Diffie--Hellman protocols with graph-based stable cubic generators from the affine Cremona semigroup \(\operatorname{End}(F_q[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n])\). This approach enables Alice and Bob to compute a shared collision tuple in \((F_q)^{n^3}\) in \(O(n^5)\) time instead of explicitly constructing the corresponding collision transformation. In this paper, we develop new implementations of twisted Diffie--Hellman protocols, as well as their inverse variants, using families of Jordan--Gauss graphs and stable generators of the corresponding affine Cremona semigroups. We show that Double Schubert graphs \(DS(k,K)\), defined over a finite commutative ring \(K\), can be used to construct stable generators of \(\operatorname{End}(K[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{k(k+1)}])\) with prescribed degree \(d\) and prescribed density \(O(n^\beta)\), where \(n=k(k+1)\). Sparse elements of \(AGL_n(K)\) are then used to conjugate these graph-based stable transformations, allowing the communicating parties to efficiently derive shared collision tuples in \(K^{n^d}\). We further show that other \(K\)-analogues of Jordan--Gauss subgraphs of projective geometry can be used in place of Double Schubert graphs to implement both the twisted Diffie--Hellman protocol and its inverse ElGamal-type variant. In addition, we investigate protocols involving two generators, one being a nonlinear graph-based transformation and the other a sparse element of \(AGL_n(K)\). Finally, we present results of computer simulations for multivariate protocols whose stable generators are constructed using the large-girth graph \(A(n,q)\).

title: Putting Large Language Models into Environmental Context
abstract: Abstract The emergence of large language models (LLMs) has fundamentally transformed information interaction, yet their application in environmental science and engineering (ESE) is hindered by multimodal data formats, dynamic context requirements, and hallucination risks. To transition from general-purpose models to domain expert agentic systems, this Perspective introduces a three-pillar framework for ESE-LLMs: domain perception, knowledge grounding, and action capability. Implementing these capabilities introduces potential pitfalls such as geographic representation bias, catastrophic forgetting, and source authenticity vulnerabilities, which require strategic model blending and careful data curation to overcome. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation must extend beyond standard knowledge benchmarks to systematically assess factuality, fairness, consistency, and safety using both human and automated metrics. Finally, we present a decision-guided deployment workflow that helps researchers in ESE fields integrate LLMs into their workflow. Ultimately, achieving trustworthy environmental intelligence relies on continuous evaluation, robust governance, and sustained interdisciplinary collaboration to safely deploy agentic ESE-LLMs for high-stakes environmental challenges.

title: Minimax rates for pointwise CATE estimation: the role of design smoothness
abstract: We study the role of design smoothness in the minimax estimation of conditional average treatment effects at a fixed covariate point. For design densities bounded above and away from zero, without further regularity, we derive upper and lower risk bounds with an arbitrarily small gap in the convergence-rate exponent. Under uniform design, we obtain matching upper and lower bounds at interior points in the regime of low nuisance smoothness. These results show that rough covariate designs can lead to slower rates than uniform designs, even under the same smoothness assumptions on the treatment effect and nuisance functions, highlighting the role of the covariate distribution in pointwise causal estimation.

title: Resource-Efficient 3D Shape and Orientation Estimation of Road Users using Roadside RGB Camera and 3D Radar
abstract: End-to-end deep learning pipelines for camera-radar 3D object detection are well established in driver assistance systems and autonomous vehicles; however, adapting them to roadside-mounted infrastructure presents significant challenges. On vehicles, sensor heights, pitch angles, and relative geometries remain largely uniform, allowing end-to-end models to generalize effectively. On the contrary, roadside sensor installations vary drastically in height, tilt, and field of view across locations, rendering end-to-end models prone to failure and difficult to adapt without massive location-specific datasets. Hence, instead of designing a complex end-to-end pipeline for direct 3D bounding box estimation, a low-cost, resource-efficient two-stage approach is proposed for real-time 3D shape and orientation estimation. The first stage utilizes any off-the-shelf, state-of-the-art method to extract 2D camera bounding boxes and associated 3D radar points for each road user. The proposed second stage then processes these inputs to construct 3D oriented bounding boxes where radar data determines 3D position, predefined templates define size for each road user, and a tiny neural network predicts a site-specific and optimized yaw angle. The algorithm is successfully validated at a curved road with a junction for pedestrians, bicycles, and cars, where it achieves 25 frames per second on an NVIDIA Jetson ORIN for real-time applications.

title: A complete quantum process model for physically realistic photo-detection in the joint photon-number and spectral degrees of freedom
abstract: Photo-detection is a fundamental component of experimental photonics, yet theoretical models often treat detectors solely in the photon-number basis, neglecting other relevant degrees of freedom such as spectral characteristics. We present a complete quantum process model for physically realistic photodetection that incorporates both photon-number effects and frequency-dependent detector response, described through explicitly derived Kraus operators in the operator-sum representation. This formalism accommodates realistic inefficiencies, models detection within finite spectral windows, and can be directly substituted for idealized models in quantum optical analyses. The model leads to identifying the suitable detection window of the detectors relative to the spectral distribution of incident photons and conversely, in order to maximize the observability of quantum effects.

title: Hierarchical Curriculum Learning for Surgical Video Generation: Focusing on Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach Robotic Thyroidectomy Datasets
abstract: High-fidelity surgical video generation is increasingly important for surgical education, simulation, and downstream AI training, as conventional simulation pipelines are limited by cost, realism, and scenario diversity. Adapting generic text-to-video diffusion models to surgical procedures remains difficult, however, due to complex anatomical structures, intricate tool-tissue interactions, the inherently hierarchical nature of surgical workflows, and the scarcity of curated training data outside a few well-studied procedures. We propose a surgical video generation framework that combines hierarchical procedural annotation with curriculum transfer learning. Surgical procedures are decomposed into three levels (phase, task, and action) and a pretrained text-to-video diffusion model is progressively adapted from coarse to fine-grained surgical context, supported by a dynamic sampling strategy that handles variable-resolution and variable-length surgical clips. We instantiate the framework on Bilateral Axillo-Breast Approach robotic thyroidectomy, a procedure for which no curated benchmark currently exists. Relative to the preceding task-level model, the final action-level model reduces FVD by 20.1% and FID by 15.7%, and a matched-budget ablation indicates that these gains arise from the curriculum design rather than from additional training. A user study with six clinicians rates visual realism highly while highlighting remaining gaps in anatomical accuracy and clinical reliability. The proposed framework offers a step toward AI-driven surgical simulation in procedures where curated data are scarce.

title: ATOM: Abstract Transition and Option Modeling - Experience-Informed Hierarchical Navigation
abstract: We propose ATOM (Abstract Transition and Option Modeling), a hierarchical navigation framework that combines higher-level graph planning with reusable lower-level option policies for efficient repeated navigation in large-scale 3D environments represented by hierarchical structures such as 3D scene graphs (3DSGs). ATOM operates on a hierarchical graph representation, implemented using, for instance, the Rooms and Places layers of a 3DSG, where each directed abstract transition is associated with a navigation option. For each transition, ATOM computes and stores a reusable option policy along with its state-dependent cost-to-go. Across repeated navigation tasks, ATOM maintains a smoothed empirical distribution over option initiation states and uses it to progressively refine the corresponding abstract transition cost. Ablation studies show that ATOM reduces cumulative repeated-planning time by 97.5% relative to a monolithic MDP baseline while maintaining trajectories within approximately 7% of a Global Places A* shortest-path reference. Experience-informed refinement further reduces abstract transition-cost estimation error by 10.3%. Physical experiments validate ATOM on an F1Tenth vehicle, successfully completing all five navigation queries with 43% of inter-region option executions reusing previously generated solutions.

title: FedCuraLM: Reliability-Calibrated and Resource-Aware Label Auditing with Small Language Models for Non-IID Federated AIoT
abstract: Federated Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) activity-recognition systems learn from decentralized wearable and smart-home records with potentially incorrect labels, non-IID client distributions, and unequal edge-device resources. Our objective is to improve downstream learning from these labels while limiting harmful corrections and respecting auditing, review, and communication budgets. FedCuraLM addresses this objective by converting sensor records into deterministic Semantic Evidence Cards, obtaining candidate-constrained small language model (SLM) assessments, and calibrating and combining them with task-model, prototype, and temporal evidence. Conflict-aware decisions retain observed labels, apply provisional soft corrections, request trusted review, or quarantine uncertain samples without overwriting annotations. Review-grounded reliability and communication-budgeted multi-prototype exchange support collaboration, while resource-aware scheduling assigns feasible SLM tiers across heterogeneous devices. Extensive evaluation on WISDM-W, WISDM-P, and CASAS using controlled symmetric, semantic-asymmetric, instance-dependent, and temporal-boundary corruption under varying client heterogeneity reveals that FedCuraLM significantly improves downstream performance over recent baselines and improves lower-tail client outcomes, audit precision, selective-correction safety, calibration, and communication efficiency. Edge-device measurements characterize latency, memory, and energy trade-offs. The findings position federated label curation as a semantic, statistical, communication, and systems problem.

title: Dynamics-Aware Gradient Clipping: Separating Feedback from Threshold Scheduling
abstract: Adaptive gradient clipping can improve training without establishing that its feedback signals are useful. We examine Dynamics-Aware Gradient Clipping (DAGC), a bounded threshold controller driven by clipping exposure and consecutive-gradient alignment. Its exposure term tightens clipping when clipping is already frequent. We show that an interior target-exposure equilibrium is unstable in a stationary mean-field model, even with exponential smoothing. We then compare the frozen controller with tuned clipping rules, an alignment ablation, and a predetermined threshold schedule on FashionMNIST and CIFAR-10, using validation-only calibration and twelve paired confirmation seeds in each of three conditions.These controls separate threshold scheduling from evidence for an online feedback mechanism; the analysis does not claim convergence of the coupled training dynamics.

title: A Gradient-Regularized Deep Learning Method for Restoring Image in Myopic Vision
abstract: Myopic vision degrades the quality of human vision due to spherical eye defocus aberrations that impair the perception of fine spatial details. To address this limitation, this work proposes a deep learning-based approach to computationally design transformed images that allow individuals with myopia in fixed distance to perceive scenes with enhanced clarity. The method trains a neural network to counteract defocus aberrations modeled using the second-order Zernike polynomial $Z_2^0$. The approach employs a U-Net architecture trained with a loss function combining reconstruction error minimization with spatial difference structural preservation through $\ell_1$ regularization. Training is carried out exclusively on the KITTI dataset, while testing is performed on DIV2K and ImageNet datasets, demonstrating generalization across diverse image distributions. Under myopic conditions modeled by $Z_2^0$, baseline performance shows visual degradation with PSNR values ranging from 19.47 to 27.42 dB across datasets and severity levels. The proposed gradient-regularized method achieves consistent improvements, delivering PSNR gains ranging from 1.48 to 7.34 dB and significantly lower perceptual compared to classical baselines.

title: PLAYGROUND: Progressive Layout Generation with Render-Grounded Planning
abstract: Generating editable graphic designs requires arranging visual and textual elements into a coherent composition while preserving their content and editability. Although recent MLLM-based approaches employ iterative generation and visual refinement to reflect the real-world design workflows, their high-level plans are predetermined prior to execution, limiting their adaptability as the design evolves. To address this limitation, we propose PlayGround, a progressive layout generation framework that dynamically adapts to the current rendered canvas. PlayGround establishes a progressive design loop comprising a Progressive Planner, a Layout Generator, and a Visual Verifier, guided by a Structure-Aware Retriever. Given an initial set of unordered elements, the Structure-Aware Retriever initially infers a coarse layout structure to retrieve structurally similar reference designs. Subsequently, at each turn, the Progressive Planner examines the current rendered canvas alongside the remaining elements, forms the next functional group, and plans its composition. The Layout Generator then predicts editable layout attributes, while the Visual Verifier evaluates rendered candidates and provides feedback when refinement is necessary. To train the Progressive Planner with step-wise supervision, we construct a two-stage data generation pipeline that extracts functional groups and turn-level planning trajectories from completed designs. Experiments on Crello and LICA demonstrate the effectiveness of PlayGround over existing methods. Our code and weights will be publicly released.

title: Deterministic Prediction as Global Velocity: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecast
abstract: Accurate uncertainty quantification is critical for many time series forecasting applications, and recent studies have increasingly adopted generative models to capture predictive uncertainty. Existing approaches often combine deterministic forecasting with generative modeling to improve predictive performance. However, their joint training is typically unstable because the deterministic model is embedded within the generative process, resulting in deep computational graphs and changing the probability transport path. In this work, we propose DV-Flow, a unified flow-matching formulation that incorporates the deterministic predictor as a parallel velocity component rather than as the endpoint of the transport path. This design enables stable end-to-end optimization while subsuming several existing formulations as special cases, allowing direct comparisons among them. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that DV-Flow consistently improves probabilistic forecasting performance over strong baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/tufts-ml/dv-flow-time-series.

title: PPVM: A Circuit Simulation Framework for Digital Twins of Quantum Processors
abstract: Quantum computers are approaching the early fault-tolerant regime. Verifying the next generation of quantum hardware requires joint emulation of the quantum processor, hardware noise, and classical control and decoding logic. We introduce the Programmable Pauli Virtual Machine (PPVM), an open-source framework for digital twins of quantum processors. PPVM unifies Pauli propagation and generalized tableau simulation under a common abstraction within a single virtual machine. Its bytecode supports arbitrary classical control flow, with measurement-conditioned feed-forward available in the generalized tableau backend. For neutral-atom hardware, we derive independent and correlated atom-loss channels and integrate them into both backends. We demonstrate loss-aware magic state distillation on over a thousand physical qubits and integration with classical decoding through Bloqade QEC Studio.

title: Revisiting Error Feedback for Model Quantization
abstract: We study causal error-feedback coefficients as design variables for model quantization. Modeling instantaneous quantization errors as independent, zero-mean variables with a common fixed variance, we formulated a metric-dependent trace problem for designing feedback coefficients. The formulation resembles fixed-order GPTQ/LDLQ feedback and supports Jacobian-aware designs that account for downstream error propagation. For a positive-definite metric $\boldsymbol{H}$, we prove that the joint rotation-feedback trace minimum is $n\det(\boldsymbol{H})^{1/n}$ and present an attaining pair using the geometric mean decomposition. Experiments on synthetic networks, trained MLPs, and language models show benefits from downstream-sensitive feedback, but also reveal that trace optimality need not improve finite-level performance. Small QAT experiments further illustrate direct loss-driven feedback tuning with fixed or trainable network weights.

title: Optimal Lower Bound on the Sample Complexity of Coherent Classical Shadows for Mixed States
abstract: We study coherent classical shadows protocols for an unknown $d$-dimensional quantum state of rank at most $r$, allowing an arbitrary joint measurement on all available copies. For observables with operator norm at most one and centered squared Frobenius norm at most $F$, we study the minumum number of copies $T$ needed for the protocol to successed with propbability $1 - δ$. We prove a lower bound on $T$, that depends both on $δ$ and the number $M$ of post-measurement observables. Denoting $\ell=\max\{\log(2M),\log(1/δ)\}$, we show that $T=Ω\left(\min\left\{\frac{\sqrt{rF\ell}}{\varepsilon},\frac{(F\ell)^{2/3}}{\varepsilon^{4/3}}\right\}+\frac{\ell}{\varepsilon^2}\right)$ under the mild assumption $\log(2M)\lesssim d\min\{r,F\}$. The lower bound nearly matches the known upper bound and matches the conjectural strengthening of the known upper bound. The proof is inspired by the framework of the proof of the lower bound for Boolean Hidden Matching. We develop a Gaussian-lift noise kernel that transfers forward and reverse Gaussian hypercontractivity to the Grassmannian, allowing us to bound the distinguishing advantage in an auxiliary game with a revealed query observable. We use Schur--Weyl structure and posterior moment bounds to control arbitrary coherent measurements on the source side.

title: A Programming, Robotics and Automatic Control Intervention for Secondary Education Students in Sweden and Italy
abstract: This study evaluates the AutoSTEM workshop, an intervention for secondary education that combines a serious game with PID-controlled hardware. Seven workshops were conducted across Sweden and Italy. The six Swedish workshops adopted an explicitly SDT-informed facilitation framework, while the Italian workshop followed the existing educational robotics format without a formally defined SDT facilitation protocol. Self-reports, an objective knowledge quiz, and qualitative responses were analysed using multiple site-adjusted statistical approaches. Technical-specific self-efficacy increased substantially in both conditions, with large effect sizes, while objective knowledge showed only modest, non-significant gains. No significant site-adjusted differences were found between SDT and control conditions for the primary outcomes. Perceived engagement was higher in the control condition, although this finding should be interpreted cautiously. The objective knowledge composite remained positive but non-significant across sensitivity analyses. Female participants reported smaller PID self-efficacy gains than males. Qualitative findings supported evidence of PID learning while identifying technical and pacing barriers. Overall, the results suggest that the technology-rich intervention supports competence development, regardless of SDT-informed facilitation.

title: Weather Forecasting and Climate Analytics Using R
abstract: Weather conditions vary continuously and are influenced by multiple atmospheric parameters, making the analysis and prediction of weather patterns an important area of data-driven research. This paper presents a study of a Weather Forecasting and Climate Analytics system developed using R programming. The system focuses on the analysis of historical weather data containing parameters such as temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed, and atmospheric pressure. The methodology includes data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, visualization, correlation analysis, and time-series analysis to identify important patterns and relationships within the dataset. The Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) model is applied to forecast future weather conditions based on historical observations and temporal patterns. In addition to forecasting, the proposed system focuses on climate analytics by examining monthly and seasonal variations, rainfall patterns, temperature trends, humidity behavior, and weather differences across different locations. Graphical representations are used to make these patterns easier to interpret and understand. The proposed approach combines statistical analysis, visualization, and ARIMA-based forecasting within the R environment to provide an integrated framework for understanding historical weather behavior and generating data-driven predictions. The study also considers limitations related to dataset quality, missing observations, extreme weather events, and the ability of traditional time-series models to capture complex atmospheric relationships. The approach can provide useful analytical support for applications such as environmental monitoring, agriculture, and weather-related planning. Keywords— Weather Forecasting; Climate Analytics; R Programming; Time-Series Analysis; ARIMA

title: TQ5CM V3 Candidate: Architecture, Mathematical Specification, and Reproducible Software Validation
abstract: TQ5CM (Transduction Quantum Cybernetic Coherence Collapse Cognitive Control Model) V3 is a frozen software candidate accompanied by technical documentation, mathematical specifications, reproducibility instructions, validation results, and epistemic limitations. The release includes a reproducible software archive and supporting documentation. According to the accompanying release record, the candidate passed the listed software test suites. These results concern the tested implementation and do not establish universal correctness, biological or neuroscientific validity, quantum mechanisms in the brain, or empirical validation. The release is provided to support reproducibility, technical inspection, and further independent evaluation.

title: Sounding Like Which AI? Machine-Style Overlap of arXiv Abstracts with Language Models of Different Vintages
abstract: We ask not how much text was produced with LLM help but how much writing, by any author, falls on the LLM side of a stylistic boundary, and which LLMs define that side. We define Machine-Style Overlap (MSO): the share of documents that a calibrated classifier on style features that ignore content-word identity judges at least as likely to be LLM output as pre-ChatGPT human writing. In 131,448 arXiv abstracts (2015–2026), MSO was 9.2% before ChatGPT and by June 2025 stood 25.4 percentage points (pp) above its pre-ChatGPT trend, far above placebo gaps. Because recent LLMs learn from recent writing, we compare generators by vintage. Against generators whose pretraining data predate ChatGPT, the gap is smaller (7.5–13.1 pp by post-trend fit; 3.5–7.6 pp for two models run from titles). Single-generator overlap mostly rose then fell, peaking later for newer generators even at equal text length (exploratory rank correlation 0.79, n = 18; 0.66 without three added post hoc). A fixed reference set, like a fixed marker-word list (delve), can show the shift receding while overlap with newer models still rises. In US school essays, English learners' essays fall in the region less often, largely because of essay scores. AI use: the study was carried out by an AI system (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) under the author's direction and is disclosed in full in the paper's Acknowledgements. The author read and approved this version. Code, data and results: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23343987

title: RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION (RAG)
abstract: Large language models are proficient with text generation but may lack factual accuracy and contain outdated information. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is proposed to enhance large language models by equipping them with external knowledge. Instead of only relying on the model's own parametric knowledge, RAG uses the information in the documents retrieved from external storage to improve the accuracy and factual correctness of the generated text. This paper reviews the RAG methods from the perspective of foundations, enhancements, and applications. We identify four foundational paradigms of RAG: Query-based RAG incorporates retrieved documents into the prompt, latent representation-based RAG fuses information in the hidden layer of the neural network, logit-based RAG adjusts the probability distribution of token prediction, and speculative RAG replaces the generation process with retrieval. All these RAG methods have unique application scenarios and are effective in different tasks.This paper also summarizes the five enhancement directions of RAG, including input enhancement, retriever enhancement, generator enhancement, result enhancement, and pipeline enhancement. Input enhancement focuses on the optimization of query formulation. The retriever enhancement covers recursive retrieval, chunking strategy, and hybrid retrieval. Generator enhancement explores the prompt engineering and fine-tuning of the generator. The result enhancement includes the optimization of the output format, and the pipeline enhancement pays attention to the system-level optimization. We present the experimental results of RAG in the fields of question answering, fact verification, commonsense reasoning, and domain-specific tasks. The experiments show that the RAG systems that can intelligently select when to retrieve and when to generate achieve better performance in accuracy and latency. The quality of retrieval is the bottleneck of the RAG system, and the optimization of each component is of significance.The RAG framework has been popular in the community and has been applied to code generation, image captioning, video description, and other fields. Experiments show that retrieving relevant documents and using the information in the documents to augment the language model is effective in all application scenarios. This survey aims to provide a global view of the RAG research field to help future works develop more reliable and maintainable AI systems

title: Data Free Training of Diffusion Models for Lattice Field Theories
abstract: Sampling equilibrium field configurations remains a major computational bottleneck in lattice field theory, motivating the development of generative samplers that can produce independent configurations. Diffusion models are promising for this purpose, but their standard denoising score matching objective requires samples from the target distribution, seemingly reintroducing the original sampling problem. Here, we show that diffusion models can instead be trained from their own generated samples using the target score identity, provided access to the unnormalized probability density. Importance-weighted formulations of this identity yield a consistent target throughout training, while unweighted variants define a self-consistent fixed-point training scheme. We benchmark the different approaches in two-dimensional \(φ^4\) theory and identify effective choices that enable efficient training and sampling across the symmetric, critical, and broken phases. Ultimately, our data-free training approach achieves comparable performance to training on HMC reference data.

title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.

title: Revisiting the Estimation of Unigram Surprisal in Computational Psycholinguistics
abstract: Contextual and unigram surprisal are standard predictors of reading time in computational psycholinguistics. While contextual surprisal is typically derived from neural language models, unigram surprisal is usually obtained from independent corpus counts. Although both quantities are deterministic functionals of a single underlying distribution---capturing conditional and marginal structure respectively---this practice breaks their probabilistic link and may introduce estimation error from the mismatch. We propose three principles for estimating unigram surprisal in psycholinguistic research, including the requirement that both quantities be derived from the same language model. We operationalize this principle by introducing a Monte Carlo estimator of unigram surprisal from a language model, along with a marginalized variant that has lower variance empirically. When unigram surprisal is re-estimated under this unified framework, we find evidence that predictors change in their predictive contribution to reading time. We also confirm prior findings that frequency can be a stronger predictor of processing effort than contextual surprisal under this unified framework.

title: Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration for Dual-Student Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Dual-student learning enriches predictive diversity in SSMIS by introducing a strongly augmented view alongside a weakly augmented view. Insufficient strong augmentation may homogenize the students, whereas excessive augmentation can corrupt anatomical evidence and destabilize collaboration. This challenge echoes feedback-regulated human instruction, where learners receive differentiated tasks and the task difficulty is continually adjusted according to their evolving responses. Inspired by these, we propose Human-Inspired Asymmetric Collaboration (HAC), a closed-loop dual-student framework that maintains weak--strong learning through adaptive difficulty calibration and geometry preservation. Specifically, Reinforcement-guided Difficulty Calibration (RDC) formulates strong-augmentation control as a window-level reinforcement learning process, using augmentation history, realized perturbations, and training responses to dynamically adjust the augmentation magnitude, operation number, and magnitude range. Meanwhile, the Gramian Geometry Preservation Constraint (G2PC) preserves the early-stage three-branch geometry through global volume and pairwise area constraints, preventing shared supervision from homogenizing the two students. Comprehensive evaluations across LA, Pancreas, and BraTS-2019 validate both the segmentation effectiveness and capability-aware difficulty calibration of HAC.

title: Saturating the Bayesian Nagaoka-Hayashi bound within numerical precision for the depolarization SU(2) rotation channel
abstract: The Bayesian Nagaoka--Hayashi (NH) bound is a semidefinite lower bound on the Bayes risk of multiparameter estimation, tighter than the Bayesian symmertic logarithmic derivative (SLD) Cramér--Rao bounds, and whether it can be attained is an open problem. We study the single-shot estimation of a qubit rotation, all three parameters at once, under depolarizing noise and a uniform prior, with $k$ parallel uses of the channel. Rotational covariance reduces the joint optimization of probe, measurement, and estimator, and the NH bound itself, to small semidefinite programs, solvable through $k=4$. At every number of uses and noise strength the optimized strategy reaches the NH bound within the numerical precision of the calculation, numerical evidence that the bound is attained for this channel family, while the SLD bound lies strictly below and is never attained. As the noise grows the optimal probe collapses to the tensored Bell state.
